modules.title: How he thinks about the game
modules.intro: His results come from a few large winners, not a high hit rate or clever chart reading. The edge he names is managing risk, executing without hesitation, sitting tight on what works, and staying in the game: no copying, no dependence on trading income, and judging the process rather than each outcome.

lessons.title: A Handful of Outsized Winners Drive the Entire Year
lessons.rule: Most of the year's profit comes from a few trades; in one count 17 trades gave about 80% of his gains and everything else kept him afloat. He cannot know in advance which trade it will be, so he keeps showing up and holds the ones that work.

how.text: He counted 17 trades contributing about 80% of his profit; the big one may come after a long stretch of little or no gain.
Expect roughly a 30% win rate and judge the year, not each trade, week or month.
Small winners take care of small losers; big winners take care of you. One or two winners fix everything.
A 10R trade gives room for 10 mistakes (18R for 18); once you stop making that many mistakes, the money flows.
Do not cap the upside: ZENTEC went 70R, 80R, then 100R+ (up 4.5x in 6 months); OLECTRA gave a 100% move in under 2 months.
Aim for large swings in a small focused set; living off 4-5% moves would require being a trading machine.

lessons.when: Across the year; the large winners cluster in good market phases.

mistakes.text: Spending hours finding a setup and closing it at 5%.
Losing focus during long stretches with little gain; the big trade can come after them.
Trying to catch every explosion instead of waiting for your own move.

lessons.evolution: 2021: he favoured small moves taken consistently for a smoother curve (1451065986921103360, 1379376714241826818); 2022: risking 1 for 10, then hunting 1:20+ (1504382197096390665, 1600730343816196097); 2024: counted 17 trades giving ~80% of gains (1770714966955286796).

lessons.title: Asymmetric Payoff: Risk 1 to Make 10 to 30, Not 1 to Make 3
lessons.rule: He risks 1 to make 10 to 30 and calls the 1:3 target old school. A few such trades pay for many small stop-outs and carry the account through bad phases.

how.text: 'I am risking 1 and going for 10' (AWL, 10% upper circuit from 352.66).
He gunned for 1:20 to 30; such trades give room for many small mistakes.
He accepts losing many 1:3 trades; stacking 1:3s would need him on his toes all day, which does not suit him.
With 1:20 you can risk small and still get good returns, which suits beginners.
To grow a small account fast: big size, which needs a small stop, which needs clean setups and precise timing; practise timing with small size.
Gains from one big trade finance the next trades, so a low win rate does not mean losing.
Why 1:5 or higher: one rough phase of back-to-back stops can wipe out all 1:3 gains made in a good market.
Even small moves are large in R with a tight stop (6.7R and 8R in a weak market).
Find 10:1 or 20:1 trades and they cover charges and bills.

lessons.when: On every trade, through tight initial risk and open-ended upside.

mistakes.text: Settling for 1:3; a choppy phase resets those gains to zero.
Widening the stop to avoid shakeouts; it then needs a much bigger move for the same R/R.

lessons.title: Trade Management and Sitting Tight Beat Chart Reading
lessons.rule: He says he makes money because he manages risk and sits tight on winners, not because of any chart style. After entry he mostly leaves the trade to the stop and the trail, because he cannot know which breakout will run.

how.text: Traders on 1-minute charts or 52-week-low stocks also make money; what they share is cutting losers and riding winners.
How much you make depends on handling the trade, not finding it; charts are only part of the equation.
Winners are right at best one trade in two; they stay small while losing and press hard and manage well when a winner shows up.
His stated edge is fearless execution: taking the next trade the same way after five losers, buying more when it is red everywhere.
Do not interfere in a trending market: some trades will stop you out, but it lands several 20-100R trades a year.
Big moves are full of scary bars (4% red days are normal); he stopped reading bar by bar and sells only at the stop or after a 30-50% move in a short time.
No price targets and no rigid view; the only things he controls are the stop and the size.
When tempted to take profits on a crumbling day, he steps away from the screen rather than interfere.

lessons.when: From entry to exit on every position, most of all in trending markets.

mistakes.text: Drawing lines and targets that cap the upside of a breakout.
Taking profits because the index or the rest of the book is falling; ask whether you really accepted the risk.
Closing a hard-found setup at a 5% gain.

lessons.title: Go Against the Crowd at Sentiment Extremes
lessons.rule: He turns cautious when the crowd is euphoric and bold when it is fearful. Extreme bearishness and rare statistical declines tell him the long side has the better odds; a move celebrated all over the news tells him he is late.

how.text: Mar 2023: Nifty down 4 months in a row had happened once in 23 years (2001), followed by a 36% rally; he said there would be more money on the long side.
Bearish talk all around is a contra indicator.
His shorthand is "scared when most are aggressive and aggressive when most are scared". Nifty at 20K dominating the headlines was his last warning before the Sep 2023 fall.
When a stock or index is up a lot and in the news everywhere, you are almost always late.
Jan 2025, same 4-month streak: he expected only a relief rally, not a new bull run.
'It is never different': the market's foundations have not changed in 100 years.

lessons.when: At extremes of sentiment: long declines with peak pessimism, or euphoric news-driven highs.

mistakes.text: Believing 'this time it is different' at a pessimistic extreme.
Buying what is already all over the news.

lessons.evolution: 2023: the 4-down-months signal called a possible new bull leg (1636023660895956996); Jan 2025: the same signal read as a relief rally only (1882011618999165374).

lessons.title: Buy Before the Obvious Breakout Point: Confirmation Has a Cost
lessons.rule: General principle: confirmation is paid for by buying higher, and obvious, good-looking points are crowded. He prefers to be in before the crowd-visible point, accepting less certainty. Execution detail lives in entries-1.

how.text: 'My edge is buying much before the obvious points.'

Confirmations have a cost: while the market confirmed, he was already 6% and then 9.4% up from the lows. Non-obvious confirmations (extreme bearish numbers, more stocks holding up than in the previous fall) let him in early.
Good-looking setups are watched by many and crowded; near-perfect but unattractive ones have performed better for him (ABB was the crowded one and failed).
Anticipating indices turning back above their MAs is an A+ skill, because future leaders move before the indices do.
A rigid wait for a mechanical follow-through day kept others out of a 1300-point rally that gave him easy trades.

lessons.when: At turns in the market and in individual bases, before the move is obvious to everyone.

mistakes.text: Buying at the obvious level and facing an instant struggle.
Waiting for index confirmation and giving up the move from the lows.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

lessons.title: Commit to One Cohesive Trading Style and Timeframe
lessons.rule: Pick a system that fits the life you live, understand its trade-offs, and repeat the same few setups. Swing trading suits him because the effort-to-reward ratio is asymmetric and it fits around a job.

how.text: Fit the system to your life: a busy job holder cannot run a day-trading system.
Know the styles: his 2025 table compares scalping, intraday, 3-day swing, swing (days to a week) and positional, with swing giving higher reward-to-risk and fitting a job at a lower win rate.
An active system gives a trade every day and grows an account with low risk, but needs more daily effort and screen time.
He swings because effort-to-reward is asymmetric, and because chasing many 1:3s would keep him on his toes all day.
Repeat a few tricks rather than learning new ones; good trading is the same things again and again.
Style is found by staying in the game long enough.

lessons.when: When choosing and sticking with a method.

mistakes.text: Shifting styles with half-baked knowledge.
Fitting your life into a high-demand system instead of the other way round.
Second-guessing a proven edge during a drawdown.

lessons.evolution: 2021: he ran and taught an active system with about a 1-day average hold (1386644073079996417); 2022: chose 1:20 swings over many 1:3s to suit his personality (1600731470112657409); 2025: published the style comparison table (1916743471014277399).

lessons.title: Process Over Outcome, Survival First, and Independent Accountability
lessons.rule: Stay in the game first, learn the skills in order, do not depend on trading to pay the bills, judge each trade by whether the process was followed, and never copy trades.

how.text: Blowing up small accounts teaches; blow up a large one and there is no next time. Stay on the crease.
Learn in order: scans, buying, selling, sizing, then spotting easy and hard days; 25-50 trades at each step, small size, forget about money.
The best time to start learning is a bad market, because it teaches defence first.
The first year builds confidence, not income; money follows confident traders.
Trade full time only without depending on it for a living, or alongside a job; being forced away from the screen helps.
Judge the process, not the outcome: winners and losers look the same at entry; a profitable bad trade is still bad.
Have your own back: no tips, no calls, no operators, no broker advice; copy the mindset, not the trades.
Question every belief that has not made you money.
Every fix creates a new problem; pick the problems you can live with.

lessons.when: Throughout a trading career, most of all in the first years.

mistakes.text: Copying a trade, then refusing to accept the stated stop and waiting for reassurance.
Depending on trading to pay bills, which breaks people in bad markets.
Outcome bias: chasing the trade that popped instead of learning the method.
Starting to learn when markets are going crazy up.

modules.title: Reading the market
modules.intro: He reads the market before he reads a chart. Daily breadth counts, where the indices sit against their short moving averages, and how his own fresh trades behave decide whether he presses, trades small, or sits in cash.

lessons.title: Market Environment Trumps Any Individual Setup
lessons.rule: The same setup pays easily in the right environment and bleeds in a bad one, so he reads the environment first. Most of the year's money is made in a short good window, often the weeks right after a correction, and the rest of the year is about keeping it.

how.text: Read conditions before the chart: a good environment with average setups is easy money; a bad environment with great setups is hard money.
His written environment filter: indices above a rising 10-day moving average, or oversold indices with fewer than 200 stocks above their 20-day average.
For a beginner, treat the market as trending when all major indices are above their 10- and 20-day averages on the daily (or the 10-week on the weekly) and limit trading to those periods.
A good environment shows up as a cluster of breakouts; a bad one as a cluster of false breakouts.
Money is made in roughly 20% of the year and preserved for the other 80%; knowing when to be aggressive and when to duck is the edge.
The easiest money comes right after 5-10% corrections; that is when he pyramids and goes for 20-40R moves. Study the month after corrections to see it.
Do not get tempted right after a crash; once conditions turn, use the gains and confidence of recent trades to press hard.
Shift gears with the tape: top gear while trends are smooth, a lower gear and no new trades when 1% down days multiply.
The same pattern depends on context: a cup and handle after a long correction (April 2023) worked far better than one after a stretched rally (June 2024).
When the environment returns he trades simply, with the daily chart and a strong start.

lessons.when: Before every new position; it sets whether he presses, trades small or stays out.

mistakes.text: Trading the same way every day, which gives back earlier gains when the market cools.
Believing that mastering one setup is enough without knowing the environment it needs.
Getting tempted to buy right after a crash.

lessons.evolution: 2022: framed as making money in about a fifth of the year (1572810375867006976); 2023 onward stated as environment over setup (1676082407269707776); Dec 2024 he wrote down a concrete filter, indices above a rising 10-day MA or fewer than 200 stocks above the 20-day MA (1869715727965622760).

lessons.title: Daily Market Breadth Tracking (The MB Sheet)
lessons.rule: He keeps a daily market breadth sheet and lets it set his aggression: too many solid green days in a row means stretched and cautious, extreme bearish days set up snapbacks. He shares it publicly and writes a note to himself in it before the open.

how.text: Columns he tracks: stocks up 4.5%+ today, down 4.5%+ today, up 20%+ in 5 days, down 20%+ in 5 days, above/below the 20 DMA (labelled the early signal) and above/below the 50 DMA; later dashboards add above/below the 200 DMA.
The sheet's own heading rule: too many SOLID greens together is not good, and vice versa.
Writes a 'note to self' in the sheet the evening before or at the open (e.g. cautious, very cautious on the long side, on the bench) and acts on it.
When breadth is stretched he plays smaller or takes no trades, and counts the money saved as a result.
Watches the count of 4.5%+ gainers in the first 15 minutes; a huge jump after a run can be the climax day, so expect a cool-off.
Charts the number of stocks above the 20 DMA against its own 20 DMA: a historical low with a stretched gap points to mean reversion.
Reads intermediate levels too: stocks above 20MA stuck at 700-800 without pushing to the 1000 zone meant no extra risk; a steady 1400 reading was not by itself a reason to close positions.
A big index fall with only a few stocks down 5%+ is noted as less damaging than it looks.
Shares the breadth page free (bit.ly link, later a Google Sheet and a Chartink dashboard) and refers members to it before trades.

lessons.when: Updated every session; the note to self is written the evening before or before the open.

mistakes.text: Punching trades every day the same way; it brings big drawdowns when the market cools a little.
Reading a very high breadth number on its own as a signal to close everything.

lessons.evolution: 2021: sheet with 4.5% movers, 5-day 20% movers and 20/50 DMA counts (1438758763956035591); 2022: added a chart of stocks above the 20 DMA versus its average (1522464200781856768); 2026: dashboard adds 200 DMA columns and is shared as a Google Sheet and Chartink dashboard (2029060839786070531, 2018535076347384148, 2034167282285613498).

lessons.title: Breadth Thrusts and Confirmed Follow-Through Days
lessons.rule: After a correction he waits for proof that buyers are back: a sudden jump in participation or an index follow-through day. He then tests with starter positions and sits longer for bigger moves, and drops the view if the low that set it up breaks.

how.text: Oct 2021: the number of stocks up 4.5%+ in the first 15 minutes jumped from 10-25 to 50+ for three days; he read it as a trend and held for bigger moves (FILATEX sold in thirds at 11R and 17.5R).
Follow-through day: the index must hold its recent low, then close up at least 1% (preferably 1.25%) on higher volume than the previous day.
Timing he gives: once the index has held its low for at least 3 sessions, a follow-through day usually lands on day 4 to 7 of the rally attempt; the rally stays valid while the FTD day's low holds.
Until the FTD he stays defensive; if the low fails or the FTD is negated, the wait extends.
After an FTD he tests with starter positions; if they do not collapse, he takes bigger risk.
An 'oops reversal' day works the same way: the view is valid only while that day's low holds; when indices broke it he went to 100% cash.

A large one-day jump in breadth (40% more stocks above the 20 DMA) is treated like a stock breaking out of a base and justifies aggression; NIFTYMIDSML400 7.62% above its 20 SMA read as bulls in charge.

lessons.when: At the end of a correction, when deciding to move from defence back to offence.

mistakes.text: Treating an FTD as permanent; he cancels it once the index breaks back below the low.
Waiting only for a rigid mechanical FTD signal; in 2023 that kept MarketSmith India waiting through a 1300-point rally.

lessons.evolution: 2021: early-session 4.5% gainer counts (1445604158489333761); Nov 2023: index FTD (1724732243917062479); Oct-Nov 2024: explicit 1% / 1.25% on higher volume rule (1851547295981961291, 1854071324974485531); Feb 2025: adds day 4-7 after a 3-day held low (1886716739716522257); 2026: a breadth jump treated as a market breakout (2107701331389726876).

lessons.title: Breadth Washouts and Extreme Capitulation Bounces
lessons.rule: When selling is extremely broad, history says a bounce follows, so he prepares a reversal list instead of panicking. If the next day does not bring a comparable wave of 5% gainers, the decline is likely to continue.

how.text: Washout markers he quotes: 800+ stocks down 5%+ (Apr 2021), 850+ (Dec 2021), 600 down on the 3rd day of a fall (Jun 2022), 700+ down more than 5% (Mar 2024 onward, with 800+ and 1000+ later).
700+ stocks down over 5%: history says the market has bounced the next day, sometimes mildly, sometimes strongly.
Check the next day: without roughly 700 stocks up more than 5%, the crash in the small/midcap space continues.
Several down days in a row averaging over 1% also set up a sharp snapback.
Look for money in stocks that are down a lot, not only in relative strength names; he keeps a separate reversal list and buys aggressively on the snapback.
Match the playbook to the move: after a hard multi-day fall look for bullish reversals; include falling knives and bottom bounces, not only breakout patterns.
After the June 2022 washout he created positions on the bounce and held them at least a day or two.
He counts deeply oversold breadth (fewer than 200 stocks above the 20 DMA) as one of the two conditions where trades work with high odds.
After a washout, money flows first to beaten-down stocks rather than to strong-RS names.

lessons.when: On climax selling days and the session after.

mistakes.text: Following media theories instead of the odds and missing the bounce.
Knowing only breakout patterns, which leaves you out of business when the market falls hard.
Hunting a fresh tight-stop long on a huge gap-up day; only those already holding make money then.

lessons.title: Breadth Divergence at Market Turning Points
lessons.rule: When the index and breadth disagree he believes breadth. An index at new highs with breadth lagging is a warning; an index at new lows while more stocks climb above their 20/50-day averages says participation is improving and a turn is near.

how.text: Nov 2022: Nifty crossed its September high while breadth stayed about 30% below its own September high.
Feb 2026: every index broke the 21 Jan low, yet stocks above the 20 MA rose from 190 to 419; he called it clear relative strength.
Mar 2026: from the lowest reading (188 above 20 MA, 243 above 50 MA) breadth improved to 259 and 385; on a -1.67% day more stocks still closed above the 20 MA.
He expected one more rapid index decline that would not damage breadth, and says it happened.
Early 2023 version: 3-month new highs vs new lows (e.g. 23/595 to 68/52), net new highs positive four days in a row even on a 1% down day, and only about 40 stocks down 5%+ on a 1-2% index fall.
Study earlier turnarounds for the same pattern: Feb-Mar 2023, Feb-Apr 2025, Mar 2026.
After breadth jumps too much in a single day, expect a cool-off that gives better days to look for longs.

lessons.when: Near index lows and highs, when headlines and price action look worst or best.

mistakes.text: Judging the market by the index alone; 'price and participation is all that matters, rest is noise'.
Taking an index high at face value while the broad list of stocks lags.

lessons.evolution: 2022: divergence noted at an index high (1591998802525057024); 2023: read through new highs vs new lows (1632775808350662659); 2026: read through stocks above the 20/50 MA at index lows (2017971714286923861, 2029060839786070531).

lessons.title: The -3% Index Shock Day: Expect Volatility Ahead, Never Buy the First Dip
lessons.rule: Every time the index dropped more than 3% in a day after a long rally, the next few days turned highly volatile, usually with more such days. A repeat would shake out any new tight-stop position, so he stops buying and lets the environment settle.

how.text: On 12 Sep 2023 he lowered his gear, took no new trades for days and posted 'Don't buy this dip. For now.'
The reasoning: the 4% drop stopped out most positions; a repeat would do the same to a new tight-stop entry. Let the environment settle the way you let a stock settle before going tight.
He kept checking the rule against later drops: a week later, Oct 2023, Jan 2024 and Feb 2024.
When 3% down days became frequent (third in under two months, Feb 2024) he took another break and used it to collect stocks showing relative strength.

lessons.when: The sessions after an index (he charts NIFTYMIDSML400) falls 3%+ in a day after an extended rally.

mistakes.text: Buying the first dip after the shock day.
Opening fresh tight-stop positions while the volatility is still playing out.

lessons.title: Warning Signs Before a Downtrend: Cutting to Cash and Stepping Aside
lessons.rule: Tops cannot be timed, but the shift from an easy to a hard market can: the same clues show up before every 5-40% fall. When they line up he cuts exposure hard, goes to cash and takes a break.

how.text: His Sep 2022 checklist: a big rally in about a month; indices extended from their averages a second time within 2-3 weeks; newest positions erasing gains quickly; his oldest, largest position stopped out; the leading name (Adani) cracking.
When the leading position is stopped out he treats it as a change of character and cuts exposure drastically (80-90% in Sep 2022, then 100% cash).
Many stops hit on one day (three in Mar 2021) is a character change: reduce risk and take a break of at least a week.
No strong follow-up within T+3 days means a trade is likely to hit its stop; he got out of almost everything ahead of the Apr 2025 fall.
Leaders tiring or showing distribution warns that the next days will be difficult for long swings: play small or not at all.
An extended market (made too much too fast) is a cue to trade very small for 2-4 weeks.
If he finds only a handful of actionable names (4 instead of his usual 10) because most are far extended, he stops buying for the week.
Before big events markets get jittery and take your stop; that is the cue to take at least a week off.
A lower high and lower low on the index, or a bear flag after rejection at the 10 MA, means no big size.
The same clues were present before the Dec 2022 pullback.

lessons.when: Late in a rally, and whenever several of these signs appear together.

mistakes.text: Punching trade after trade after many stops hit together.
Staying in through a big event and taking the larger damage that follows.

lessons.title: Consecutive Green Days: Trend Power at the Start, Exhaustion at the Top
lessons.rule: Six green days in a row is a poor moment to buy the next day, but its meaning depends on where it appears: after a long downtrend it marks a powerful new trend; after a long rally it is a warning.

how.text: Six straight up days is bad for buying the next day.
When the streak follows a long bad trend, at the start of a new trend, it is a very powerful sign (NIFTYMIDSML Mar-Apr 2023, WELSPUNLIV, HBLPOWER).
The same streak after a long rally becomes bad.
His breadth sheet carries the same idea: too many solid green days together is not good, and vice versa.

lessons.when: Whenever an index or stock strings together many up days.

mistakes.text: Treating every green streak as overbought without asking where in the trend it appears.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

lessons.title: Base Counting Applied to Indices and Commodities
lessons.rule: Base count works on indices and commodities as on stocks: rallies lose momentum after the 3rd base and the odds of failure rise after the 4th, and the same logic works on the way down, independent of news or fundamentals.

how.text: Every rally becomes erratic after the 3rd base; after the 4th the odds of a U-turn rise. The same logic works on the downside.
Mar 2026: NIFTYMIDSML400 was 4 bases down, pessimism was at its peak and breadth had stopped deteriorating, so he went aggressively long.
He inverted the index chart so the fall reads like a familiar uptrend: largest bar, rally 4 bases old, so expect a reversal; he still kept status yellow with 20-40% exposure for 3-4 days.
Same count shown on Gold futures and the Nifty Realty index: '4 bases fall'.

lessons.when: During extended index or commodity moves, on daily and hourly charts.

mistakes.text: Waiting for crowd confirmation; for him an asset already 3-4 bases down is confirmation in itself.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

lessons.title: Your Own Positions and Stops as the Primary Market Thermometer
lessons.rule: His fresh trades tell him more than any index. His good trades usually work instantly; when they stop doing so, or even tiny positions get hit, he reads the market as lacking easy money and steps back.

how.text: Before 18 Oct 2021 almost every other trade moved 3-5R instantly; when the last 5-6 did not, he stopped trading for the rest of the week and avoided the 400-600 point fall.
'My good trades usually do well instantly': no thrust for an hour or a fading move means trim or close.
Breakouts with no follow-through: trade ridiculously low size until a few hits in a row; when even the smallest positions fail, take a day or more on the bench.
Before pyramiding he gives his first buys a day or two to say add more or cut to zero.
Remove indices from the screen; watch open positions, which can stay strong and make new highs on heavy index down days.
When a few trades round-trip he keeps his exit rules and shrinks size until breakouts start working again.

lessons.when: Every session, through the behaviour of new and open positions.

mistakes.text: Watching the index all day.
Continuing to add new trades when even the smallest positions are failing.
Changing sell rules to take smaller gains because a few trades came back.

lessons.evolution: 2021: the instant 3-5R test (1453229062365798402); 2022: feedback from first buys decides pyramiding (1565666989838041088); 2026: states explicitly that feedback changes size, never exit rules (2105520694343913664).

modules.title: Market-condition playbook
modules.intro: When the market looks like this, this is what he does.

conditions.name: Breadth Thrust / Follow-Through Day (Rally Launch)
conditions.reads: A sudden jump in breadth after a quiet stretch: in Oct 2021 he counted stocks up 4.5%+ in the first 15 minutes, which went from 10-25 a day to 50+ for three days running. On the index he looks for a follow-through day: Nifty up at least 1% (preferably 1.25%) on higher volume than the day before, after the index has held its low; in one post he adds it usually comes 4 to 7 days after the low holds for 3 days.
conditions.does: Sits for bigger moves instead of booking small gains, increases new positions, and is willing to give back recent gains to test whether the market can take more risk. In the Nov-Dec 2023 run he pyramided (four entries in COCHINSHIP) while saying the pace was not sustainable and he was ready for a dip. He also watches for the thrust to climax: on 18 Oct 2021 a huge jump in 4.5%+ stocks made him expect a cool-off.

periods.note: 50+ stocks up 4.5% in the first 15 minutes for three days; he sat for bigger moves and had a double-digit month in 10 days, then flagged 18 Oct as a possible climax.
Follow-through day on 15 Nov; he increased new positions, pyramided COCHINSHIP, and by 7 Dec said he was prepared for a dip.

conditions.name: Sustained Trending Market
conditions.reads: Every index is above its 10 and 20 MA and 1000+ stocks are above their 20 MA (his Jan 2026 description of one of the best swing-trading conditions). Leaders keep bouncing off their moving averages; he wrote that in a true bull market you can trust the averages. The contrast case: stocks above the 20 MA stuck at 700-800 for days meant the market lacked the push to reach the 1000 zone.
conditions.does: Does not interfere with working positions ('not the market to choke good positions'), holds leaders as they surf their 10/20 MAs, adds to leaders, and sells some into sharp spikes. In the spring 2023 rally he still cut size across the portfolio by a set percentage on 5 May rather than picking winners.

periods.note: Once selling pressure lifted, BSE kept surfing its 10/20 MAs; he got five 10-to-100R trades that month (BSE, RIIL, MIRZAINT, KITEX, CLEAN).
Nifty up 1000 then 1300+ points with no formal follow-through day; he called these some of the easiest trades and trimmed size across the book on 5 May.
Every index above 10/20 MA, 1000+ stocks above 20 MA; 'not the market to choke good positions'.

conditions.name: Late-Stage Exhaustion and Breadth Divergence at Highs
conditions.reads: The index makes a new high but breadth does not (Nov 2022: Nifty above its September high while breadth stayed about 30% below its own). Other signs he lists: indices extended from their averages for the second time in 2-3 weeks, a lot made too fast, breakouts not sticking or fading several days in a row, leading names extended, his big winners pulling back, and new positions giving back gains quickly.
conditions.does: Trades very small to keep gains, stops adding new risk or benches himself, sells part of extended positions, and moves toward cash (15 Dec 2022: 'stay light' to members).

periods.note: He had made a lot fast and saw an extended market; traded very small. On 18 Mar three positions closed the same day and he benched himself for at least a week, then watched a 1%+ down day from outside.
Nifty near highs while stocks outside the Nifty 50 deteriorated; on 15 Dec he told members to stay light and moved toward cash.

conditions.name: The 3% Index Shock Day After a Long Rally
conditions.reads: A one-day drop of more than 3% in the index (he charts the MidSmall 400) after a long rally. His study: every time it happened, the following days turned highly volatile and often brought more such days. In Feb 2024 he counted three of them in under two months.
conditions.does: Lowers his 'gear' and takes no new trades for a few days, does not buy the dip, lets the environment settle before tight-stop entries, may take a break, and collects stocks showing relative strength (in Sept 2023: names trading above the 12 Sep high).

periods.note: MidSmall 400 fell about 4% on 12 Sep; he had already lowered gear, said not to buy the dip, used the 12 Sep high as the RS filter, and noted another 3% down day on 23 Oct.
MidSmall 400 down 3.14% on 23 Jan; on 12 Feb, the third such day in under two months, he went on a break and collected RS names.

conditions.name: Extreme Breadth Washout
conditions.reads: A day when 700-800+ stocks fall more than 5%; he says history shows a bounce the next day, sometimes mild and sometimes strong. He checks the follow-up: after 13 Mar 2024 he said the crash would continue unless around 700 stocks rose 5%+ the next day. Very low readings of stocks above the 20 MA (about 190 on 21 Jan 2026) became the reference he measured later divergence against. After four down months on Nifty (Jan 2025) he expected a relief rally.
conditions.does: Does not sell into the flush; prepares a reversal list and takes small reversal plays with tight stops (e.g. BPCL with a 1% stop, small size, the day after the March 2024 washout). Holds strong positions, which in Dec 2021 gapped up 3-8% on the bounce.

periods.note: 800+ stocks down 5%+ on 20 Dec; he said odds were high for a bounce, Nifty bounced 200 points, and his leaders gapped up 3-8% next day.
700+ stocks down 5%+ on 13 Mar during a small/midcap crash; he expected many reversal plays and took a small BPCL reversal the next day.

conditions.name: Choppy, Rotational Environment
conditions.reads: Frequent 2% gap-down days and chop in between; most breakouts fade or show no follow-through; trades go nowhere for hours. In 2022 he showed stocks above the 20 DMA swinging up and down with trends not lasting, and called it a typical stage 3.
conditions.does: Switches to tight-stop trades: about 1% stops, risking 0.2-0.4% of the portfolio, average hold around one day, getting out early and selling into strength. Uses time stops (closed DEN and BRITANNIA after 3+ hours of no movement). Plays very small until he gets several good hits in a row, and skips days when breadth is already extended.

periods.note: Many 2% gap-down days; 1% stops risking 0.2-0.4%, average hold one day; +5.83% over 30 days.
Breakouts with no follow-through; traded very low size until a few hits came in a row.
Most breakouts fading; small positions with 0.5-1% stops and quick exits.

conditions.name: Clustered Stop-Outs / Leader Stopped (Character Change)
conditions.reads: Many stops hit on the same day (or in the same week) is a change of character for him. So is his oldest, largest leading position getting stopped out, or recent new positions erasing gains quickly. He also notes markets get jittery before big events and take out stops.
conditions.does: Takes a break, usually stated as at least a week; cuts exposure sharply (Sept 2022: by 80-90%, then 100% cash). On returning he tests with small toe-in-the-water trades and builds only if feedback is good, otherwise extends the break. In July 2024 he set a rule in advance: 2-3 more trades at smaller size, and a one-week suspension if those also lost.

periods.note: His largest position (stopped 12 Sep) was the trigger; he cut exposure 80-90%, went to cash and benched, then avoided a ~5% Nifty fall.
Profitable positions retraced to their stops on 19 Jul; he planned smaller trades then a one-week suspension; on 13 Aug, with only 700-800 stocks above the 20 MA, he declined to add risk for a week.
Stopped trading on 6 Mar after back-to-back stops; MidSmall fell 9% from peak while he was down 4.98%.

modules.title: Choosing stocks
modules.intro: How he picks what to trade: relative strength in falling markets, price that ignores bad news, early-stage stocks, avoiding extended ones, strong sectors, leaders that respect their moving averages, young low-float names with enough liquidity, repeat attempts on stocks that stopped him out, a short focus list, and price over fundamentals.

lessons.title: Relative Strength Shows Up When the Market Falls
lessons.rule: Corrections are when relative strength is easiest to see. Stocks that do not go down with the market - up on a red day, holding above the 20 MA, back at their old highs, or making new highs while the index falls - are the names to collect, and some become leaders of the next move. He judges RS by eye against the index, not by a rating, and a stock showing RS is not automatically a buy the next day.

how.text: Embrace corrections and gap-down days: use them to spot relative strength.
When the market starts correcting, collect names that are up today, still above the 20 MA, or bouncing back to their old highs.
After a shock day, stocks trading (or that have traded) above that day's high have RS - e.g. above the 12 Sep 2023 high.
When every major index has an outside day, stocks with an inside day (e.g. LODHA, GNFC) have RS.
New highs on a heavy down day are the clearest tell: JISJALEQS on a 1% down Nifty day, JUBLINGREA and CONFIPET (5%+ up on a 1%+ down day), MIDHANI on a deep red day.
A stock hitting a new 52-week high while the market is at a 52-week low 'can't be a fluke' (ZENTEC, Mar 2023).
Judge RS with your eyes against the index; some of his biggest wins had RS ratings under 50.
Keep a list: during volatile phases he steps back from trading and collects RS stocks, which is where future gains come from; he shares such lists.
After a rally, note which stocks rose 2x more than the market in the same period and focus on those.
RS feeds entries: ZENTEC was chosen for its strong sector, 5-day RS and history of fast moves; PENIND and MRPL entries cite RS on a negative day.

lessons.when: Market corrections, gap-down days and sharp sell-offs.

mistakes.text: Treating a stock that held up today as a buy tomorrow; RS names don't necessarily start going up right after the fall pauses.
Only buying stocks with an RS rating above 90.
Watching the index instead of the stocks.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the idea from 2021 to 2026; he added ways to measure it over time - the shock-day high in 2023 (2023: 1704711888041304237) and leaders of a rally at 2x the market's move in 2026 (2026: 2074842373675536847).

lessons.title: Bad News, No Fall: Price Diverging From Bad Results
lessons.rule: A stock that stays positive or barely reacts to very bad results or bad news is telling you the news is not negative to the large money. He calls this divergence between bad news and price action his investment indicator, and watches for it every earnings season; it has given him conviction to buy and to hold.

how.text: In earnings season, watch which stocks stay positive even on very bad results.
IRB: net profit down 87%, stock up 1% with no spike down and a clean setup; next day 4%+ up on strong volume.
PDMJEPAPER: earnings down 108% over the weekend, no negative reaction on the next working day, setup stayed clean.
IDEA went 8% up on bad news and was later 70% up; SJVN fell only 3.5% on a CBI case when he expected 10-20%, then made a new high; Laurus Labs closed up 5% from the lows on a 90% profit fall.

Use it for conviction in your own trades: the TTML divergence gave him confidence to hold 109,000 shares; he flagged SUNTECK ('I can smell money here') before buying it; MOL and TRIVENI were other examples.

It applies to supply events too: GROWW's anchor lock-in selling was fully absorbed by 10:30, and capital-market stocks ignored STT noise - one reason he sized up, with price action as the deciding factor.

lessons.when: Results season and any day with company-specific bad news.
lessons.evolution: The idea appears in Jan 2021 as his 'new investment indicator' (2021: 1351087421199437824) and he kept using it in the 2023-24 results seasons (2023: 1718870682912649456, 2024: 1751223040199782692); in 2026 he applied it to an IPO lock-in expiry (2026: 2021445617781006732).

lessons.title: Life Stage of a Stock: Buy Seeds and Saplings, Not Mature Trees
lessons.rule: He compares a stock's life stage to a tree's - seeds, seedling, sapling, young tree, mature tree. Big moves come from the seed and sapling stage, often a first base breakout early in stage 2; by the fourth base a stock is unlikely to go much higher. Check which stage you are buying before you buy.

how.text: Map the stage: seeds/seeding (the base), sapling (the breakout), young tree (the run), mature tree (the late, steep part).
Prioritise stocks at the seed/sapling stage; corrections throw plenty of seeds at you.
Before buying, check whether it is a seed or a mature tree and play accordingly; the concept applies on every timeframe, 1-minute to monthly.
What an early-stage leader looked like (MIRZAINT, 2021): stage 2, first base breakout, multiple 20+ million volume weeks.
Young trends are a reason to buy: RIIL was chosen because it was a young trend; a '5 star' setup is a young move after a long base with breakout volume in millions and surfing the MAs.
Count bases: 3 bases old with the latest the shortest is no longer young and reversals are common; it is highly unlikely to go much higher from base 4.
Real-time seed buys he cited: MIDHANI, ITCHOTEL, HBLENGINE (seed turning into sapling).
The same applies to sectors: in 2025 he said defence was no longer a young space and to find the next one.

lessons.when: When evaluating any base before entry.

mistakes.text: Entering late bases; he says smart positional traders do not.
Getting caught in extended, mature moves.

lessons.evolution: In 2021-23 he described it as stage 2, young trends and base count (2021: 1466296801082839043, 2023: 1676128995585171456); from Jan 2024 he used the tree life-cycle analogy (2024: 1750064208534773909) and reshared it in 2025 (2025: 1925483424187560092).

lessons.title: Avoid Extended Stocks, Even When They Look Tight
lessons.rule: Tightness is an entry point, not proof of quality - study the base and the cause instead. A tight setup sitting far above its moving averages after a vertical run is extended; he will not trade it until the averages catch up or price pulls back. And he says to stop buying stocks that are up three days in a row.

how.text: Extended = a rise of 30-50% in 3-5 days, or a rise at an angle of 80-90 degrees; such moves stall or fall flat.
Stop buying stocks that are up 3 days in a row if you want better odds from the start.
A very tight pattern far above the averages is still extended: wait until the averages catch up or price pulls back.
He showed what happened: buyers of that extended breakout sat at breakeven for 6 days, then 17 days.
He declined a follower's 'superb tightness' TATAINVEST chart and later noted it was still going nowhere.
Judge quality from the base and the cause; strong causes create strong effects.
When most of his list is far from its base, he stops buying: in Feb 2024 he found only 4 actionable names because everything else was super extended.

lessons.when: Whenever a setup looks tight after a fast run.

mistakes.text: Treating tightness as the only selection criterion.
Buying a breakout in a stock already massively up 3 days in a row.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets; in 2022 he noted the extension definition and the 3-days-up rule dated back to 2019-2020 (2022: 1518500002729172992, 1518501164756914176).

examples.caption: AMARA RAJA daily, 29 Nov 2022: a gap-up vertical run in early November from ~520 to ~640 (purple dots), then two weeks of tight bars around 640-646 with a red dashed breakout line - buyers flat for 6 days.
Unlabelled daily chart he posted asking 'Will you trade this?': a base, then two big up days and a steep climb, then tight small bars far above the base.
A follower's TATA INVESTMENT daily (Nov 2022): a climactic Sep run on heavy volume to ~2,900, a drop, then a narrow range near 2,300-2,400 - the 'tightness' he declined.

lessons.title: Trade the Sectors and Themes That Move Together
lessons.rule: When most stocks in one sector move together you get really big moves, so sector analysis is a big edge. He looks for groups moving up in unison, picks the strongest names in them, prefers strong sectors even for reversal plays, and steps aside when a sector's leaders crack.

how.text: Do the sector analysis: four consumer-finance names up 50%+ in a month together; logistics up together with his GATI trade the strongest.
Know which theme is playing: after every correction in 2021, real estate fired up within days; PRESTIGE was picked partly for its strong sector.
Group moves he flagged: Adani stocks, oil stocks, mining (RAIN with GRAVITA, NMDC, HINDZINC, HINDCOPPER), pharma, packaged food, metals, graphite, railways, capital markets.
Group RS: mining stocks made new highs by a huge margin without the market making new highs; 7 of 8 had exploded and he built a KIOCL position from it.
Play the strongest merchandise in the group, including for SS/reversal trades.
Prioritise reversal plays in strong sectors (steel, finance, construction in Dec 2022) - 'playing strong sectors is an extra edge'.
Use sector strength as an entry reason (BANCO, PENIND) and sector weakness as an exit reason (closed TNPL as the entire sector struggled).
He has a video on finding leading sectors and stocks.

lessons.when: Any time a group starts moving together, especially out of corrections.

mistakes.text: Staying in a sector after its leaders crack; he stays away when the leading names 'sneeze' and warned laggards fall more when the leader cracks.

lessons.evolution: No change in the method; the sectors change: consumer finance and real estate in 2021, steel/finance/construction in late 2022, mining in 2023, metals and oil in 2024, graphite and railways in 2025, capital markets in 2026 (2021: 1363481831841157123, 2022: 1607099437452599296, 2023: 1700023653897781434, 2024: 1841765947863859519, 2025: 1947151389169209770, 2026: 2021504198735692056).

lessons.title: Leaders Respect Their Moving Averages
lessons.rule: In a true bull market leading moves almost always bounce off their moving averages, and that is a sign to spot one. Stocks that have never, or barely, closed below their 50 MA in the last 50 days have an established trend and are likely to bounce after a pullback. The first touch of the 20 or 50 MA after a strong move is often an easy trade - but you buy it with your own setup, not on the touch.

how.text: In a true bull market you can trust the moving averages; leading names respect their MA zones.

Established-trend scan: stocks that never (or barely) closed below a chosen MA, say the 50 MA, in the last ~50 days; they are likely to bounce back after a pullback and suit pullback trades for working people.
Real example: ZENTEC barely closed below its 50 MA in 100 days, and he rode it for over 80 days.
Breakouts 'surfing 10/20' and young trends that start to surf the 10/20 MA are the ones he saves and rides.
First touch of the 20 or 50 MA after a strong move: put the name on your focus list, watch it, and strike with a setup you trust (SVRO, VCP or your own).
Expect it to be messy: the stock may hover around the MA for a while before resuming, as APOLLO did.

lessons.when: Trending markets, for stocks already in strong moves.

mistakes.text: Buying the moment the stock touches the moving average instead of waiting for your setup.
Expecting a clean touch-and-bounce every time.

lessons.evolution: The 50-MA established-trend scan appears in 2021 and again in 2023 with ZENTEC (2021: 1457708107891576834, 2023: 1659907859608379393); the first-touch idea is spelled out in 2025 (2025: 1960718632083714526).

lessons.title: Young, Low Free-Float Stocks With No Overhead Supply - and Enough Liquidity
lessons.rule: In 2021 he said trading started working for him only when he invested in young, low free-float companies with a strict stop policy. He checks free float on the BSE site rather than scanning for it, likes names with no overhead supply in the past year, and matches liquidity to his size; surveillance moves that drain liquidity get him out.

how.text: Prefer young, low free-float companies; combined with pyramiding and concentration this is how his account grew in 2021.
No free-float scanner needed: check the free float on bseindia.com; if it is under Rs 5,000 crore go for it, otherwise drop it.
No overhead supply to the left in the last 1 year was common to multibaggers he bought (IBVENTURES, BEPL, GOACARBON, GRAPHITE, SUNFLAG); use it to discard names.
Large-float stocks move less: on KOTAKBANK he booked half at 2.5R and did not expect fireworks.

Liquidity scales with account size: average volume at least 50x your desired quantity, a minimum average rupee volume of say Rs 10 crore (he uses much more), and double the threshold if you face slippage.
He does not trade BSE-only stocks because volumes are lower than NSE.
When a stock is moved to T2T or ASM surveillance, liquidity dries up and he exits (MIRZAINT: 70,000 of 2 lakh shares traded were his; NIITLTD; ITI).

lessons.when: When choosing which names to put on the list and how much size they can take.

mistakes.text: Hunting for a free-float scanner.
Assuming big names are safe; without an exit plan all stocks are equal on the downside.
Trading a stock that trades only ~10k shares a day at large size - fills and exits get expensive.

lessons.evolution: 2021: low free float was central to his approach (2021: 1354988704570302468). The no-overhead-supply rule is from 2019, reshared in 2024 (2024: 1859155941037420911). 2024: exits forced by T2T/ASM surveillance (2024: 1753272580402823468, 1864525112893968554).

lessons.title: Don't Delete a Stock Because It Stopped You Out
lessons.rule: Deleting a stock because it stopped you out is the amateur mistake. Each failed attempt shakes out weak hands who rarely come back, so the next attempt has fewer hurdles. Keep watching stocks that stopped you out, and if they set up again, prefer them over a new name; he makes multiple attempts in the same stock.

how.text: Each drop throws out a few weak hands, so every new attempt has fewer hurdles; eventually the stock zooms, mostly without you if you stopped watching.
Weak hands who burned their fingers don't return, which makes 2nd attempts more powerful than the 1st and 3rd more than the 2nd.
Given the choice, he picks a setup that just had a shakeout over one with none.
Treat a stock squatting after a breakout as normal, and as another add opportunity if it makes a new attempt.
If a stopped-out stock sets up again, go for it over a new name: GENUSPOWER's big shakeout with no follow-through selling gave it priority.
He re-enters the same names: 2nd attempts on DIXON, DEEPAKFERT (smaller size), OLECTRA and KIOCL; a net profit on PFOCUS after 3 attempts in 4 days; JAYNECOIND traded three times in a year.
Being stopped out before a big move is part of the business: he does not care, and keeps watching (GOLDIAM).

lessons.when: After any stop-out in a stock that still has a good structure.

mistakes.text: Deleting or cursing a stock because it stopped you out - 'you were the weak liquidity for strong players'.
Stopping at one attempt and moving to a new stock.

lessons.title: A Narrow Focus List, Scanned Rarely
lessons.rule: Scans are not his edge; a focused list is. He builds a short list of names with liquidity, speed, clean consolidations and a history of big moves, reviews it, and updates it every week or two instead of scanning daily. Over the years the list got shorter and his scanning rarer.

how.text: Compile scan results into a main focus list and review it every evening; after a few weeks the list is long enough that you no longer need daily scans.
Stop once you have ~10 actionable names; he reviews 200-400 stocks (about 20 in weak markets) and deliberately stops there.
Keep a limited universe - around 50 stocks chosen on strength, performance, liquidity and sector (2024).
Build a focused list of no more than 10-20 names with liquidity, speed, clean consolidations and a history of big moves (2025).
Trim the list by asking whether the stock can still deliver a 30-50% move; anything without a convincing yes comes off.
Scan once every two weeks to update the list; trade a handful of stocks over and over.
A focus list of about 20 quality names, given time to set up, beats scanning hundreds of new stocks every day.

lessons.when: Weekly or fortnightly list maintenance; the list is traded in between.

mistakes.text: Running scans every day; he calls it injurious to performance and 'anxiety wearing a blazer'.
Running in every direction by looking at 1,000+ stocks a day.
Asking which scan he used when your scan didn't show his names.

lessons.evolution: The list shrank and scanning became rarer: 2023 - review 200-400 stocks and stop at ~10 (2023: 1665616410729492484); 2024 - a universe of ~50 (2024: 1801473388235346016); 2025 - 10-20 names (2025: 1958008843733995682); 2026 - scans rarely, every two weeks, a handful of stocks traded repeatedly (2026: 2008771383678169280, 2023646819021197807).

lessons.title: Price Over Fundamentals, Valuations and Ratings
lessons.rule: For swing trading he does not check fundamentals: price and volume are enough. Many stocks rise 40-50% with zero earnings, stories and turnarounds move prices too, and high-PE growth stocks can keep rising. Late rating downgrades often arrive near the lows rather than predicting further falls.

how.text: He does not check fundamentals for swing trades; price and volume are enough.
Stop demanding good recent earnings as a swing/momentum trader; many stocks go up 40-50% with zero earnings.
Don't question why momentum is going up; by the time you get the answer you will likely have missed the move.
Earnings and management quality are not the only drivers; stories, hope and turnarounds move prices too, and price behaviour gives the heads-up earlier.

Valuation does not cap a momentum move: GRAPHITE went from PE 100 at 350 to PE 220 at 900; APOLLO from PE 60s at 100 to 160s at 350. Short term runs on euphoria and fear; long term returns to fair value.
Late downgrades often mark lows: Moody's downgraded UPL after a ~50% drop and it stopped going down; the IT big four rose 50% after being downgraded.

lessons.when: Whenever evaluating a momentum candidate.

mistakes.text: Letting a fundamentals box stop you from taking a pure momentum trade - 'too much information for momentum investing'.
Treating an exam or registration heavy on fundamentals as proof someone can make money in markets.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: TCS weekly (2020-2024): a measured 56.94% rise from the Sep-2022 low to a new high near 4,500 by Sep 2024 - his example of IT stocks rising after downgrades.

modules.title: Setups
modules.intro: Manas Arora names a small set of recurring setups: tightness (VCP, 3WTC, WIB, base on base, tennis ball), Strong Start (later SVRO) and ORB, range breakouts, buying inside the base, Reversal Plays and falling-knife/mean-reversion trades, oops reversals, MA pullbacks in leaders, selling-climax ranges, squats, and earnings breakouts. In 2021-22 he also shorted extended moves and wrote deep OTM calls. Where his tweets do not state a setup's mechanics, the lesson says so.

lessons.title: VCP: Buy When Each Pullback Gets Smaller
lessons.rule: He buys a strong stock whose swings keep shrinking - he calls it contracting or reducing volatility, and names the cleaner versions VCP - entering just above the tight area with the stop just below it.

how.text: Look for successive pullbacks that shrink: his OIL chart marks -14.89%, -9.85% and -4.32%, and his NIITLTD hourly chart -14.2%, -7.4% and -3.3% into the same level.
The tell he names on NIITLTD: on the third attempt the stock 'stopped going down like it used to'.
Entry above the top of the extreme tight zone, stop below it (ACE: 'Entry above blue line. Stop below the red line').
The pattern can be read on intraday frames: he executed ACE on 15-minute bars, OIL on a 1-hour box, and his trade notes use VCP60 for a VCP on the 60-minute chart.
He uses it as one of the trigger systems for names on his focus list, e.g. after a first touch of the 20 or 50 MA.
Labelled examples: FACT ('contracting volatility'), COFFEEDAY ('textbook VCP breakout?'), IREDA ('Classic VCP'), CUB ('VCP trade').

lessons.when: No market condition is attached to the VCP itself in the tweets.

mistakes.text: Knowing the pattern is not the edge: he says anyone can learn SVRO or VCP and the game is won by controlling behaviour.
A VCP breakout late in a move can fail; he shorted Nifty on what he called a classic late-stage VCP breakout failure.

lessons.evolution: Described as contracting volatility from 2021 (2021: 1405093270649065473, 1444938245456809986); the VCP label and VCP60 shorthand appear more in 2025 (2025: 1927298081655050593, 1990035299003740598). The setup itself does not change.

examples.caption: OIL: daily chart with three measured pullbacks of -14.89%, -9.85% and -4.32% along a rising line, and a 1-hour panel with a small shaded box he bought out of.
NIITLTD 1-hour bars: three pushes to the 205.87 line with pullbacks of -14.16%, -7.37% and -3.33%, his 'reducing volatility' reason.

lessons.title: WIB: Weekly Inside Bars
lessons.rule: WIB stands for weekly inside bars - a style he says he traded a lot in 2016-2018 and still posts as a trade reason. Inside bars only show a contraction; the move comes from strong buying that happened before the contraction.

how.text: Tags new positions simply 'WIB' (SEQUENT, AVTNPL, GATI in 2021; AEGISLOG in 2025).
His stated rule on inside bars: they only indicate a contraction in volatility; without strong buying force before it, an inside-bar breakout usually fizzles.
He wrote a thread on telling a good weekly inside bar setup from an average or bad one and points to it as how he would trade WIB; its contents are not in this archive.
On SEQUENT he added a second lot at 179 on a base-on-base breakout and planned a 4-8 week hold.
AEGISLOG was narrowed down the evening before and entered at 831 with a 2% stop.

lessons.when: Not stated in the tweets.

mistakes.text: Treating an inside bar by itself as the signal: without strong prior buying force it tends to fizzle out.

lessons.evolution: He says WIB was his main style in 2016-2018 (2025: 1876568329399472151); it appears as a trade reason in 2021 and again in 2025. No change in method is described.

examples.caption: SEQUENT weekly bars, 4 Jan 2021: a steady advance above a rising line, with the latest week's range sitting inside the previous week's near the highs - tagged WIB.
GATI weekly bars, Feb 2021: a sharp Nov-Dec advance, then several narrow weeks hugging a rising average line - tagged WIB.
AEGISLOG weekly thumbnail: a run of small overlapping weekly bars sitting on rising average lines.

lessons.title: Clean Breakouts From a Range or Big Base
lessons.rule: Many of his entries are stocks moving out of a sideways range or a large base; he calls the good ones 'clean breakout' and warns that breakouts that do not follow through get closed fast.

how.text: Trade reasons he gives: rising trend, higher lows and a tight range (RTNINDIA).
Labels follow-ups 'clean breakout from the range' (LODHA) or 'clean breakout' (NSLNISP, NLCINDIA).

Prefers stocks coming out of a big or large base; on OLECTRA he noted resilience in a market dip and that it historically gives monster moves; on PENNAR, relative strength on a negative day and taking out the day high.
His filter from 2023: every breakout win had a rising 20 MA on the daily with entry above it, and a narrow previous day.
In very strong markets he prefers the high-to-mid area of a base and leaves low-cheat entries alone; he marks a mid-area line and considers the setup only above it.
Stops are stated on each post (LOD, 1%, 2% or a fixed level), and starter positions are added to later (LODHA starter 920 then breakout; NSLNISP added at 46.75).
Also names smaller patterns as reasons: mini cup & handle (PNBHOUSING).
Keeps 'textbook breakout' charts in a study file (EIHOTEL, MINDTREE).

lessons.when: He links breakout odds to the environment: breakouts work better when most stocks are above their 20 DMA.

mistakes.text: Holding a breakout that does not follow through: he closed RTNINDIA after two days without follow-through and LEMONTREE as a 'bad breakout'.
Expecting full fills: on continuation breakouts he often gets only part of the order.

lessons.evolution: The rising-20MA plus narrow-prior-day filter is stated in May 2023 (2023: 1660164680743272448); the high-to-mid area preference is stated for strong markets in 2025 (2025: 1902283670796345702).

lessons.setup: In-base entry before the crowd (NATIONALUM / MIRZAINT style)
lessons.title: Building a Position Inside the Base Before It Shows Up in Scans
lessons.rule: Some of his biggest trades were pieced together inside a base, around congestion areas on a smaller time frame, before the daily chart looked clean and before the stock appeared in breakout scans. He says it is not his bread-and-butter setup.

how.text: NATIONALUM: pieced together 94,500 shares at ~94.70 over several days around congestion areas on a smaller frame; once it moved, it would appear in every scan (high volume, 1-month high, 5%+).
Repeated the approach the same day with a first buy in GLENMARK with a 1% stop.
RAMASTEEL (stop 35.7 on 36.7) and MIRZAINT (stop 47 on 48) were starter positions he describes as on the lines of NATIONALUM; he calls it not his bread-and-butter setup.
TTML was built up over several days for the same reason; a divergence between bad results and price action gave him more confidence to hold.
He links these catches (NATIONALUM, MIRZAINT, RAMASTEEL, NCC) to his thread comparing a stock's life to a tree's life cycle from seed onward, and asks readers to guess the stage he caught them at.
On MIRZAINT he stresses the size was his usual size and the trade was nothing special - execution, not stock finding, is the point.

lessons.when: Not stated beyond the examples (Dec 2023 - Feb 2024).

mistakes.text: Waiting for the move to show up in scans: by then it is crowded - spot it before.

lessons.title: Reversal Play: Buy the Turn After Excessive Weakness
lessons.rule: 'Reversal Play' is his label for buying a strong stock (or index) after a run of down days, at the point the fall turns, with a very tight stop - usually the low of the day - and often small size. He prefers it in stocks already in strong momentum and in strong sectors.

how.text: PRESTIGE, his worked example: 5 down days in a row, huge recent buying interest, strong sector; the decision was made pre-market and executed after watching a minute or two; 1% stop, small size.
Stops posted on these entries are LOD, 0.5-2%, or a fixed level a point or so below entry.
Size is often 'small', 'small bet' or 'testing water' on the first attempt.
Play it on the strongest merchandise: stocks already in strong momentum and strong sectors (steel, finance, construction named in 2022); not on stocks whose structure is broken.
A smaller-frame version: the stock undercut the low of its range and reversed with speed (ADANIPORTS).
Why he likes it: best bang for the buck on risk/reward, and you can do size because the majority is selling, so orders fill easily.
He picks the days from market breadth: when the market falls too hard for days in a row he looks for bullish reversals, and on a washout day he prepared a reversal watchlist.
The same idea is applied to index futures and options, executed on a lower frame after a daily oversold and breadth read; stop LOD or 15 minutes, whichever first.
Can combine with a strong start ('Reversal Play + SS', ELGIEQUIP).

lessons.when: After sharp declines and in choppy or weak phases: in March 2023 he said it was not the market for breakouts but for reversals/pullbacks, when most stocks were below their 20 DMA.

mistakes.text: Playing reversals in weak stocks: he contrasts strong-momentum names with a long downtrend chart, and warned KPITTECH reversal players that its structure was broken.
Some reversal entries fail the same day (UTTAMSUGAR in a market where moves were failing); the LOD stop keeps it small.

lessons.evolution: Present throughout 2021-2025 under the same label. From Dec 2025 he increasingly calls the crash version 'mean reversion' and uses the two names together (2026: 2016089967437742160) - see the mean-reversion lesson.

lessons.title: Leaders Surfing the 10/20 MA
lessons.rule: A leader that rides its rising 10- and 20-day averages after breaking out is his '5-star' set-up; he buys or adds near those averages with tight stops and keeps holding while it keeps surfing them.

how.text: His 5-star definition: a young move after breaking out from a long base, breakout volume in millions, a strong uptrend surfing the MAs (TALBROAUTO).
Entry examples: PRESTIGE pilot buy - institutional buying, surfing 10/20, strong sector, stop LOD; BSE bought at 1460 with a 0.5% stop while it surfed the 10MA.
Keeps 'textbook breakout surfing 10/20' charts in a file (ADANIENT, BSOFT).
In a true bull market, great leading moves almost always bounce off the moving averages; he adds there (NCC 4th entry around the 20 DMA; ZENTEC bounce off 20MA; ABB reversed from the rising 20MA).
A bounce off the 20MA with volume, or a shakeout and bounce off the 10MA after earnings, is read as true leadership and an add point (JAYNECOIND, ATHERENERG).
Holds the remainder while the stock keeps surfing 10/20 (RIIL, CLEAN, MIRZAINT, THERMAX).

lessons.when: Strong, trending markets: 'In a true bull market, you can trust the moving averages.'

mistakes.text: Jumping into a set-up he labelled 'in progress' - he calls that dumb money.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets; the '5-star' phrasing is from Dec 2021-Apr 2022 (2021: 1470247989432111106; 2022: 1490907832941973504) and the same MA-bounce language returns in 2026 (2026: 2048704954861519001).

lessons.setup: First touch of the 20/50 MA after a strong move
lessons.title: First Touch of the 20 or 50 MA After a Strong Run
lessons.rule: After a strong run, the first pullback to the 20 or 50 MA is often an easy-money trade - but the touch only puts the stock on his focus list; he still waits for a trigger setup (SVRO, VCP or another system).

how.text: First touch does not mean buy at the touch: put the name on the focus list, watch closely, then strike with a setup you trust.
The stock will not always touch and bounce; it can hover around the average for a while and then resume (APOLLO).
Oil stocks at the 50 DMA for the first time after an extremely strong run-up: potential for big moves if that base holds; he later entered OIL.

ChartGym rules on extended names: after a ~50% rally with turnover up 300%, wait for an undercut of the 10 MA (NAVINFLUOR); after 66% with turnover doubled, wait for at least a 20 MA undercut (GESHIP); BSOFT considered only once it undercuts the 10 MA.
A run of names pulling back to the 10MA after an 8-week uptrend is the real test of a rally; holding and bouncing strongly suggests a longer next leg.

lessons.when: In strong markets after a leg up.

mistakes.text: Buying the moment the stock touches the moving average instead of waiting for your own trigger.

lessons.evolution: The 50-DMA first-touch idea is posted in 2024 (2024: 1777927949900976357), the 20/50 first-touch rule with a separate trigger in 2025 (2025: 1960718632083714526), and the extension-based undercut rules in his 2025-26 ChartGym threads (2026: 2030619643275260034, 2033184245716603142).

lessons.rule: He used the label 'PowerPlay' once, for a third entry in PCJEWELLER after a roughly 4-week rest that followed a fast advance. The tweets do not state the rules of the setup.

how.text: PCJEWELLER: third long entry at 26 after a rest of about 4 weeks, tagged PowerPlay; earlier buys at 15.5 and 18.5.
What the chart shows: an ~85% advance in about two weeks, then a sideways rest above a rising average before the add.
He framed the trade as buying, buying more and sitting tight; it reached 85% from his first buy in 7 weeks.
He cites it as an example of low float + pyramiding + concentration.

lessons.when: Not stated.
lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets; the label appears only in Jan 2021 (2021: 1346017804911136768).

lessons.title: Strong Start (SS), Upgraded to SVRO
lessons.rule: 'Strong start is the new breakout': he buys a prepared candidate on day 1 of the move when it opens strongly with heavy early volume, instead of waiting for the obvious breakout level. In June 2025 he said SS was upgraded to SVRO; he does not spell out what changed.

how.text: Two ingredients of a good breakout candidate: the strongest start, and a clean consolidation with no wild bars (HAPPSTMNDS: gap-up opening + clean consolidation).
Enter on day 1 of the move rather than at the obvious breakout point later (RADICO 1 vs 2; BSE punished late comers).
Early volume as backing: KITEX and BSE did about 25% of average daily volume in the first 10 minutes of the breakout day.
Entries tagged SS are posted with tight stops (1%, 2 points, LOD) - INDHOTEL, NIITLTD, OBEROIRLTY, CHOLAFIN, DHAMPUR.
Related tags on entries: 'Open = Low day', 'ORB', 'Gap-up + ORB' (ORB = opening range breakout).
Combines with other reasons: 'Earnings + SS', 'Reversal Play + SS', small base on base + strong start (NTPC).
RVOL matters: he skipped an entry because 'RVOL missing'; the Strong Start RVOL dashboard credits him for the concept.
Use that dashboard only on a focus list of 7-10 names already studied - scanning the whole market just creates FOMO, and SS execution has to be very quick.

SVRO: 'SS just got upgraded: SVRO'; trade notes use SVRO15 / SVRO3 for SVRO on 15-minute and 3-minute charts; he presented his 'SVRO entry tactic' at a conference. The mechanics of SVRO are not described in the tweets.
Play SS on the strongest merchandise.

lessons.when: In good markets: 'just the daily chart and looking for a strong start is enough' (May 2026). In the weak Feb-Mar 2023 tape he took no strong-start trade for over 40 days.

mistakes.text: Buying the obvious breakout after the move instead of day 1.
Running the RVOL dashboard on the whole market: no prior study, no conviction, FOMO entries.
A strong start can still fail the same day (BRIGADE).

lessons.evolution: Coined 'Strong start is the new breakout' in Dec 2021 (2021: 1467461224908541954); ORB and Open=Low tags appear in late 2024 (2024: 1841001172225646864, 1854385688034115914); renamed/upgraded to SVRO in June 2025 (2025: 1930524085617938594); RVOL dashboard used on a small focus list in 2026 (2026: 2074870533817311632).

lessons.title: Earnings Breakouts and Kicker Gaps
lessons.rule: A big jump in sales (ideally sales and EPS) can start a multi-quarter uptrend, and he buys some results-driven gaps on the day ('kicker', 'Earnings + SS'). He also says that in Indian markets, because of circuit filters, it is usually better to watchlist an earnings breakout and enter later. He does not use the term 'Episodic Pivot'.

how.text: His 2018 rule, reposted in 2022: a loss-making or slow-growing company delivering a 40-100% jump in sales (preferably sales and EPS) in the recent quarter, or at least 20% annually, could start an uptrend lasting a few quarters - not a signal to enter right away.
ITI: after a close to 100% jump in sales it gapped up into a 'rare KICKER pattern' with volume up 600%+; stop at the pre-gap level.
Same-day entries tagged 'Earnings + SS' (SRF, LOD stop) and 'Earnings breakout + SS' (APOLLOTYRE, 2% stop, starter position; 425 the next day).
But: playing the earnings breakout on results day is not for our markets because circuit filters stop 100-500% same-day moves; keep the stock on the watchlist and enter later, as he did with AMBER.
He questions whether trading the quarterly announcement itself helps.

lessons.when: Earnings season.

mistakes.text: Assuming the results-day candle is the whole opportunity: circuit filters cap it, so the better entry often comes later.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets; same-day earnings entries appear in 2021-2023 alongside the 2023 caution to enter later (2023: 1661268977962688513, 1722122995064340619).

lessons.title: Oops Reversal: When a Panic Gap-Down Reverses
lessons.rule: His 'oops' entry is a reversal back up after a weak or gap-down open. He also uses the idea defensively: on gap-down days caused by noisy events he waits the first 3-4 minutes before executing stops, because the stop level can turn into a buying point.

how.text: JUSTDIAL: pilot buy at 601, stop 590, labelled an 'Oops' entry he had used before in an ADANIENT trade.
On noisy-event gap-down days, wait the first 3-4 minutes before closing at the stop; he published an OOPS REVERSAL indicator for such days (JIOFIN example).
He accepts that waiting adds some risk and calls it worth taking to avoid exiting strong stocks too early; on a panic day he said the method saved many positions.
Marked as a second entry in a trend: ChartGym NAVINFLUOR '2nd entry oops reversal' near the 10 MA.
A weak close negates it: after calling 'classic oops reversal behaviour' in ANGELONE, DATAPATTNS and J&KBANK, he said the closing was not good so it was negated.

lessons.when: Panic or noisy-event gap-down days.

mistakes.text: Selling at the stop in the first minutes of a noisy gap-down, only to watch it reverse.
Treating it as confirmed before the close: a weak close negates the reversal.

lessons.evolution: Used as a pilot entry in 2022 (2022: 1582989147949527040); from mid-2025 also as a rule for executing stops on gap-down days, with an indicator (2025: 1950770816720805979; 2026: 2034486231351128349).
