lessons.setup: Falling knives / excessive weakness / mean reversion
lessons.title: Catching Falling Knives: Mean Reversion After a Sharp Fall
lessons.rule: He deliberately buys excessive weakness - falling knives - where the fall slows down, because the risk/reward is better and size is easy to get while everyone sells. From Dec 2025 he labels these #MeanReversion and treats them as short bursts: take the risk multiple and walk out.

how.text: Selection (Dec 2025): the biggest decliners, far stretched from their averages, sitting at key support and highly liquid. The trigger is a fresh low the next session followed by a fast reversal (DIXON, INDIGO).
Every falling knife slows down at some point and that is what he tries to catch; the R/R is better and you can do size because the majority is selling.
Every rise or fall gets stretched and snaps back; the point is identified by studying history.
Can buy in anticipation without waiting for a level when the fall is extended on both the daily and a smaller frame (JSL on 30-minute, NYKAA).
Exits: the whole point is short bursts of strength - book the risk multiple the same day or within one or two days; sold some and trailed the rest.
Size small: 'not my pitch to hit sixes'; keep trades small while learning.
Also applied to index futures (Nifty after a gap-down stretched the band; Nifty Mar fut 2026) and combined with SVRO for execution (ANGELONE futures, 1% stop).
Keep it in the repertoire: traders who only know breakout patterns are out of business for long stretches after a crash, when falling knives are plentiful.

lessons.when: After crashes and panic sell-offs (Dec 2025 fall, Jan-Mar 2026), and on days breadth flags as stretched.

mistakes.text: Expect many stop-losses at first while learning the timing.
Treating them as long holds - they are short bursts.

lessons.evolution: In 2021 he framed it as buying 'excessive weakness' against the buy-strength consensus (2021: 1440166448496713739, 1451069354120859649); from Dec 2025 the same trades are tagged #MeanReversion with explicit selection and exit rules (2025: 1999008658475331797, 1999332137015869773).

examples.caption: LTTS daily, 21 Jan 2026: a long decline below the 10/20 averages, a large gap-down candle on the results marker, two more red days, then a green candle with a long lower wick (purple marker) - his mean-reversion entry.
ADANIPORTS daily, 5 Jun 2024: a huge red candle on election-result day, then a reversal candle from ~1,160 (green arrow) closing at 1,354.6.

lessons.setup: Selling climax with no follow-through / base count
lessons.title: Selling Climax, No Follow-Through, Then a Range
lessons.rule: After a decline, the largest down bar (a selling climax) that gets no follow-through and is followed by a tight range is his trigger, usually executed on the 1-hour chart with the long bias already set on the daily. He also counts bases: a fall that is 3 bases old makes the next sharp drop a climax bar for him.

how.text: Bias from the daily, execution on the 1-hour chart (GROWW).
GROWW: 'Selling climax (largest bar)', then 'price in a range for 4 hours'; entry on the bar breaking out of that box, stop LOD.
NETWEB: a large sell-off, no follow-through and a tight range; bought above the high of the range bar.

IRCTC: the largest fat bar on the 1-hour frame was key; ideal execution was the break of the 1-hour range with a stop below the box, but spotted after the close he bought next morning with a stop below the first bar.
HSCL described the same way: climax sell-off followed by no follow-through and a range.

Base count: rallies lose momentum after the 3rd base and failure odds rise after the 4th; on SHIPROCKET the fall was 3 bases old, so the sharp drop was his climax-bar entry; GAJA showed the same story.
The same base-count logic in reverse appears in 2021: he bought PAYTM after its 4th selling wave.

lessons.when: Pullbacks and declines where he already has a long bias on the daily chart.

mistakes.text: Waiting for confirmation at a breakout level: he says find the confirmation on the day he entered instead - and it is not just many red bars in a row.

lessons.evolution: Base-count buying is shown on PAYTM in 2021 (2021: 1461210194378067970); the climax / no-follow-through / range trigger is spelled out in 2026 (2026: 2021157475269935614, 2044635236093575223, 2094674334480814251).

examples.caption: GROWW 1-hour chart: a drift lower, the largest red bar labelled 'Selling climax (largest bar)', a small box labelled 'Price in a range for 4 hours', and a large green bar breaking out of it.
NETWEB 1-hour chart: a shaded 'large sell off', small bars labelled 'no follow through sell and a tight range', 'Bought above high of this' at ~3317, then a run to ~3,700.
SHIPROCKET 1-hour chart: three shaded down-bases under a falling average, then a sharp red bar annotated 'This bar was my entry trigger... sharp fall after 3 bases is climax bar for me'.

lessons.setup: Squat (long upper wick) then clearing it
lessons.title: Squats Are Not Always Bad
lessons.rule: A breakout that 'squats' - closes well off its high with a long upper wick - often scares weak hands out. If the stock does not fall after it and then takes out the squat's high, he treats that as a valid entry, and says it can be added as a setup.

how.text: NIITLTD: long wicks scare away those who do not understand; they throw weaker hands out and let the stock move freely on the next attempt; he added at 206.4.
If price does not fall after the long wick, take the trade.
INDRAMEDCO squatted on day 1, then crossed that high, as NIITLTD did; later it cleared all squats and made new highs.
Squat, no follow-through, then a strong start the next day: 'that's one set-up you can add to your basket'.
SUVEN (2026): he entered on a big red-wick bar inside the base precisely because newcomers would not take it.

lessons.when: Not stated.

mistakes.text: Assuming a long upper wick means the breakout failed - he uses that fear to enter.

examples.caption: NIITLTD daily, 26 Nov 2024: two long upper wicks in November (purple line) with his note that they scare away weak hands, then a +13.6% day on ~487% relative volume.
SUVEN daily: an August recovery, a red bar with a long upper wick (purple marker) inside the base, then a large green breakout bar.

lessons.title: Tightness and 3WTC: Buy Strong Stocks When They Go Tight
lessons.rule: 'Buy strong stocks when they go tight' is the principle he says has not changed. 3WTC (three weekly tight closings) is the weekly version he tagged on many 2021 entries; on the daily he looks for a cluster of very small bars and enters early with a tight stop. He also warns that tightness is only an entry point, not what makes a stock strong.

how.text: Tags entries '3WTC (Weekly Tight Closings)': IIFL, GEOJITFSL, KPITTECH, a second CAMLINFINE lot.
His older filters for good 3WTC setups (reposted 2022): the whole range of the latest week under 10% is a big plus; prefer two-digit stocks; free float under Rs 5,000 crore.
Find an extremely tight formation and enter 'early'; entering only after a level 4-5% away gives up the easy low-risk money.
Tight stop trades need impeccable timing; a tight stop does not mean low conviction.
A very rare bar showing extreme tightness can be bought above its high with a tight stop.
Daily examples: GNFC and FLUOROCHEM ('how tightness looks like'), ANGELONE (3 tight closings on the daily, added).
Tightness is not responsible for the quality of the breakout - study the base and the cause; strong buying force beforehand leads to stronger moves.

lessons.when: Not stated.

mistakes.text: Selecting stocks on tightness alone - it has become a fad and fools traders; it does not define the stock's power.
Entering after the move instead of early inside the tight area.

lessons.evolution: Heavily used as 3WTC in early 2021 (2021: 1352552887067402240); from late 2022 he adds the caution that tightness is only an entry point and the cause matters more (2022: 1593220327668355072; 2025: 1958414293126320378).

examples.caption: IIFL weekly bars, 22 Jan 2021: a big November thrust on heavy volume, then a shaded box of three weeks closing close together near 114-116 as the rising average catches up.
GNFC daily, 27 Apr 2021: a Feb-Mar run, a two-month range, four very small bars circled, then a +10.9% expansion day on higher volume (green arrow).
IIFL weekly bars posted as an 'easy money set-up example': narrow weekly closes resting above a rising average after a high-volume surge.

lessons.title: Base on Base
lessons.rule: He names 'base on base' as a trade reason: a new base forming on top of an earlier one, bought as it breaks out.

how.text: SEQUENT: second long at 179 with the note '4 to 8 weeks + Base on Base Breakout'.
NTPC: bought at 135 because it had set up with a small base on base and a strong start; it gapped up the next day.
RKFORGE: entry with stop LOD, reason given as 'Base on Base'.

lessons.when: Not stated.
lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: SEQUENT weekly bars, 4 Jan 2021: a shaded 3-4 week base just under ~179 sitting above an earlier advance, with the current week pushing through its top.
RKFORGE weekly candles, Feb 2023: after a 2022 base, three shaded boxes stacked one above another - each base forming on top of the previous one.

lessons.setup: Tennis ball (bounce off the previous base)
lessons.title: Tennis Ball: Bounce Off the Previous Base
lessons.rule: 'Tennis ball' is his name for a stock that breaks out and then bounces straight back off the top of its previous base; he used it as a reason to add a second lot.

how.text: PRINCEPIPE: second long at 291, 'bouncing from the previous base (Tennis ball)'.
He listed two tennis ball trades as an example of having a few tricks you are great at and repeating them.

lessons.when: Not stated.
lessons.evolution: No clear change; the term appears only in early 2021 (2021: 1351376395495038976).

examples.caption: PRINCEPIPE daily, 19 Jan 2021: a December breakout above a purple line at ~283.6, a pullback that holds the line, and the bounce he added on at 291.

lessons.setup: Shorts: extended move / parabolic / bearish reversal / stage 3
lessons.title: Short Setups: Extended Moves and Bearish Reversals
lessons.rule: In 2021-2022 he shorted extended stocks after weak or failed breakouts, parabolic moves when breadth was stretched ('bearish reversal - inverse of buy reversal trades'), and slow stage-3 tops full of false breakouts. He calls shorts not his bread and butter and by 2023 describes himself as long-only.

how.text: ADANIENT short: extended move (main reason), lethargic post-breakout reaction, failed breakout, failure to cross the breakout point - then the strike; he suggests looking at the inverted chart.
JSWSTEEL short: an already stretched move broke out without enough rest; the failed breakout confirmed the view.
Parabolic short DWARKESH around 124.30 with a 1-point stop when breadth was stretched; MARUTI bearish reversal short at 7388 with a 20-point stop.
Stage 3 short TVSMOTOR: a slow stage 3 full of false breakouts after a strong stage 2 rally, expecting stage 4.
Time stops for longs do not apply to shorts - a top takes time to crack, like the stage 3 to stage 4 transition.
Preparation rule: market up too fast - sit out or look for bearish reversals (not his bread and butter).

lessons.when: When markets or stocks are stretched to the upside, or a stock is in a choppy stage 3.

mistakes.text: Exiting a short just because it is slow to work - tops take time to crack.

lessons.evolution: Shorts appear in 2021-2022 (2021: 1397172420755083272; 2022: 1501787247603220480); in 2023 he says short trades tend to be quick, offer worse risk/reward and distract him, and that he focuses on long-only (2023: 1665616417230667776).

examples.caption: ADANIENT futures daily: a near-vertical run from ~500 to ~1,330; numbered points 1-4 near the top mark the sluggish breakout, failed breakout and failure to recross ~1,335 before the short.

lessons.title: Writing Deep Out-of-the-Money Calls
lessons.rule: In Sep-Oct 2021 he wrote deep out-of-the-money calls on stocks as 'easy money trades for call writers': the risk/reward is never good, but the probability of profit is high.

how.text: VOLTAS: sold the 1300 CE at 16 with spot at 1215; the premium fell even while spot rose, and he covered at 1.75.
GODREJPROP 2400 CE fell from 40 to 6; TATAPOWER 210 CE was his first wrong one and he planned adjustments with a new OTM strike.
His framing: R/R never good, money in absolute terms almost certain.

lessons.when: Not stated.

mistakes.text: Ignoring that the R/R is poor: one wrong trade (TATAPOWER) needed adjustment.

modules.title: Entries
modules.intro: Entry execution, as he describes it: buy before the obvious point, do not chase extended moves, start with a pilot or starter position and add only on good feedback, act early in the session with the plan made before the open, set the bias on the daily and execute on a lower frame, re-enter stocks that stopped you out, check results dates, and do not rush to buy the first dip after a sharp index fall. Pyramiding is covered in trade management.

lessons.title: Buy Before the Obvious Breakout Point
lessons.rule: His stated edge is buying much before the obvious points. With tight-stop trades he enters early inside the tight area; waiting for a level 4-5% away gives up the low-risk money, and the move usually starts before the breakout candle everyone sees.

how.text: Find an extremely tight formation and enter early; entering after a level 4-5% away will not give easy low-risk money.
A clean setup that has been tight for two days is itself a confirmation; the breakout is just the obvious-to-the-eye one, and waiting for it has a cost.
Place bids after the supply has dried up.
Enter on day 1 of the move, not at the obvious point where late money buys (RADICO).
'My edge is buying much before the obvious points' - illustrated with PNB Housing: 'I'm buying here' at ~375 versus 'a rookie buys here' at the ~408 breakout line.
Find the confirmation on the entry day itself rather than at a later level break.
Do not draw hurdles everywhere and keep hesitating - if buying above a hurdle is your breakout, there are hurdles everywhere.
Squats and scary red wicks inside a base are used to enter because newcomers will not.

lessons.when: Constructive bases in strong stocks; see the setup lessons for specific triggers.

mistakes.text: Waiting for the breakout candle: experienced traders know the move usually starts before it appears on everyone's screen.
Waiting for index confirmation: he was up 9.4% from the swing lows by the time indices confirmed.
Ignoring a name while it is boring on the watchlist, then chasing it when it gives FOMO.

examples.caption: PNB Housing daily: a June spike high at ~408.7 marked 'a rookie buys here & faces instant struggle', and a September entry lower in the base at ~375 marked 'I'm buying here'.
SUVEN daily: a long upper-wick red bar inside the August base (purple marker) that newcomers feared; he entered, and a large green breakout bar followed.

lessons.title: Do Not Chase Extended Moves
lessons.rule: Buying after a 20-25% rise in a few days is good setup, bad timing: with a tight stop it will usually stop you out. Time the entry before or right at the beginning of the move.

how.text: Chasing a stock that is already up 25% in three sessions usually means the trade starts out losing; a run of 10 up days in 11 is the same mistake of a good setup at a bad moment.
With a stop of around 2%, you cannot buy a stock up 20% in 3 days; it will hit the stop 9 times out of 10.
Moves run 3 to 5 bars on average; aim to get in on the first or second bar, and check what the 2-3 bars before your entry did.
Prefers 20% in 20 days over 20% in 2-3 days - the former lets him load up without risking much.
A near-90-degree move on your trading frame kills the stock for a while; retail enters after it and loses (ZENTEC).
FOMO is the hint that the position cannot be managed with a tight stop - you are already late.
A rally of ~20% in 4 days into a swing breakout level makes that breakout poor risk-reward (JAMNAAUTO, 2020).

lessons.when: Fast momentum phases where FOMO is high.

mistakes.text: Jumping into a setup labelled 'in progress', or buying the obvious level after the run (BSE late comers).
Waiting for your scan to show the mover and buying it after the move - wait for scan results to go tight on a later date.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets; the same rule is stated in 2021 (2021: 1440971696593195011) and 2023 (2023: 1638103319448092673).

examples.caption: RADICO daily, Dec 2021: label 1 at the first strong day off the range low (his entry) versus label 2 at the obvious breakout high after the run, where he says late money buys.

lessons.title: Pilot / Starter Position First, Add Only on Good Feedback
lessons.rule: Many new positions start as a 'pilot', 'starter', 'small size' or 'testing water' buy with a stated stop. He gives the first buys a day or two to show whether to add or cut to zero, and only builds on them if the feedback is good.

how.text: Posts label entries 'Small position. Testing water.', 'Pilot position. Will add more if it acts well', 'Very small size. Hope to add more', 'Starter position'.
Toe-in-the-water positions are not for the gains: they check the market's pulse; build on them if feedback is good, otherwise exit and take another short break.
The most important ingredient before pyramiding is feedback from open positions: a day or two for the first buys to say add more or cut to zero.
Examples of adding after the starter acted well: DATAMATICS small size at 311.5 then full size at 314; ASTERDM doubled on follow-through; VBL bought more.
Starter stops are stated in the post: LOD, 1%, 2%, or about one rupee/point below entry on low-priced stocks (NSLNISP 44.9/43.9, MIRZAINT 48/47, MRPL 72.8/71.8).

lessons.when: Standard for new trades, and especially when testing the market after a correction.

mistakes.text: Building on a toe-in-the-water position when the feedback is bad, instead of exiting and stepping back.

examples.caption: MRPL daily, 12 Aug 2022: after a collapse from the June high near 124, a month of flat trading around 70-74; small pilot entry arrow at the top of the flat range (stop 71.80).

lessons.title: Enter Early in the Session, With the Plan Made Before the Open
lessons.rule: His own data showed trades taken before 10 am won about 45% of the time against about 20% for trades taken between 12 and 2 pm, and acting on it reduced his drawdowns greatly. Entries are planned before the open and executed quickly.

how.text: Win rate before 10 am ~45%, dropping to ~20% between 12 and 2 pm; collect your own data like this.
He says this insight reduced his drawdowns 'to a great great extent'.
Decision made pre-market, executed after watching for a minute or two (PRESTIGE); LAURUSLABS executed in the first few seconds.
JISLJALEQS bought in the first few minutes with instant gains; several trades became risk-free the same day.
Plans entries before the open with a basket order ready; says GTT orders are unreliable and to use basket orders instead.
If he misses the open he may buy after a slight pullback (NCC).

lessons.when: Every trading day.

mistakes.text: Taking fresh entries in the 12-2 pm window, where his win rate was about 20%.

lessons.evolution: The time-of-day statistic is from 2021 (2021: 1443519340117053446); basket-order planning appears in 2025 (2025: 1915263702816756157). No change in the principle.

lessons.title: Bias From the Daily, Execution on a Lower Frame
lessons.rule: He decides on the daily chart and uses a lower time frame (1-hour, 30-minute, 15-minute or 3-minute) only to time the entry and place a tight stop.

how.text: 'Strong on daily. Execution on a lower frame.' - ACE entered from a tight 15-minute zone.
GROWW: the long bias was already made on the daily frame; the 1-hour chart was used just to execute.
Index longs: oversold daily and breadth set the bias, execution on the 3-minute chart after a second shakeout.
IRCTC: ideal execution was the 1-hour range break with the stop below the box; spotted after the close, he entered next morning with the stop below the first bar of the day.
OIL: daily contractions, entry on a 1-hour box; his notes use VCP60, SVRO15 and SVRO3 for 60-, 15- and 3-minute triggers.
His workspace shows weekly, daily, 1-hour and 15-minute panels of the same stock side by side.

lessons.when: All entries; in a good market he says the daily chart plus a strong start can be enough on its own.
lessons.evolution: Already practised in 2021 (2021: 1444938245456809986); the 'bias on daily, 1 hour just to execute' wording is from 2026 (2026: 2021157475269935614).

examples.caption: OIL: the daily chart with shrinking pullbacks on top, and the 1-hour panel below with the small shaded box he bought out of.

lessons.title: Re-Enter Stocks That Stopped You Out
lessons.rule: Do not stop watching a stock after it stops you out. If it sets up again, he prefers it over a new stock: the shakeout removed weak hands, so there is less profit booking on the way up, and every new breakout attempt tends to be stronger than the last.

how.text: Every new breakout attempt is more powerful than the previous one; it can give another trade idea and the confidence to buy extra (TATASTEEL attempts 1-2-3).
ZENTEC worked on the third attempt; he says he goes heavy if it sets up again after throwing weak hands out.
Why: the new attempt has fewer weak hands (like you), so less profit booking on the way up; buy it over a new stock.
Test before re-entering: would you buy it here if this were your first attempt?

Re-entries use the same tight stops (1%, 2%, LOD) and are tagged 'Re-entry', '2nd attempt' or 'another attempt' (SWSOLAR, INDIAMART, ISEC, KIOCL, IRFC, DELHIVERY, GPPL, ITI, PRESTIGE, OLECTRA, AEROFLEX).
A day-one exit is not final: KALYANKJIL was closed at the close with no cushion, noting he might enter again tomorrow.

lessons.when: Quality stocks that stopped him out but keep setting up.

mistakes.text: Abandoning a stock after it stops you out - most stop watching it.

examples.caption: TATASTEEL daily: a May high at ~1,247 (dashed line), then three numbered attempts at that level in July; the third launches a run toward ~1,450.
KIOCL daily, 10 Oct 2023: after a September breakout and a first attempt in early October, a large red day and then a green turn-up candle with the re-entry arrow near 310.

lessons.title: Check Results Dates Before Entering
lessons.rule: If results are due, he does not carry a fresh entry into them: on BAJFINANCE he noticed earnings were that day and closed immediately, and on ADANIPOWER he closed the same day after missing that results were due the next day.

how.text: BAJFINANCE: bought at 8130 with a LOD stop, noticed 'Earnings today', closed.
ADANIPOWER: 'Didn't check earnings due tomorrow. Will close it today itself.'

lessons.when: Earnings season.

mistakes.text: Not checking the results date before buying - both examples were caught only after entry.

examples.caption: BAJFINANCE daily, 17 Oct 2023: a steady advance to ~8,200 and a tight pause; the entry arrow is on the day carrying the purple 'E' results marker.

lessons.title: Do Not Buy the First Dip After a Sharp Index Drop
lessons.rule: After a 3%+ one-day index fall following a long rally, he expects the next days to stay volatile and does not rush to buy: 'Don't buy this dip. For now.' Let the environment settle the way you let a stock settle and go tight.

how.text: Every time the index dropped more than 3% in a day after a long rally, the following days turned highly volatile, often with more such days; a fresh tight-stop position will not survive a repeat.
Posted 'Don't buy this dip. For now.' on 12 Sep 2023 and followed with the intraday chart continuing lower.
When 3% down days became frequent (three in under two months) he took a break and instead collected stocks showing relative strength for future gains.

lessons.when: Right after a sharp index decline that follows a long rally.

mistakes.text: Putting on new tight-stop positions straight after a 3%+ index drop.

modules.title: Risk and position size
modules.intro: Manas sizes every trade by what he can lose rather than by what he buys: a small slice of the account behind a tight stop, which lets him take large positions. He cuts size, then stops trading, when losses pile up, takes breaks after clusters of stopped trades, presses size only when his recent trades and the market are working, and sizes so that no overnight gap can do lasting damage.

lessons.title: Risk a small, fixed slice of the account per trade
lessons.rule: Every trade risks a small, predefined fraction of the portfolio. In his 2021 tight-stop phase that was 0.2-0.4% per trade against his usual 0.5-1%, and open risk across the book only once or twice reached 0.5%. Risk is the distance to the stop times the quantity, not the size of the position, and the stop is simply the most he is willing to lose.

how.text: Fix the rupee risk first: e.g. a Rs 10 lakh account, 10% in a stock with a 2% stop = Rs 2,000 = 0.2% of the portfolio.
Judge exposure by what you can lose, not by how big the position looks; he bought Rs 1.36 crore of stock while risking Rs 64,000.
Report results as % of portfolio and as multiples of risk (e.g. ZENSARTECH: portfolio +3.1% while risking 0.25%; six tight-stop trades at 0.2% risk made 3.35% in 10 days).
Beginners: limit each loss to 0.5% of the account and review after every 10 trades whether to risk more or less.
Raising risk per trade later multiplies the result of the same trades (he notes his usual size is 0.5-1% risk).
The stop is the maximum he is willing to lose, with no other logic; put it in the system and exit at it without fail.

lessons.when: Every position he opens.

mistakes.text: Looking at the size of the position instead of the loss it can cause.
Not exiting at the stop, or keeping stops only in your head.
Thinking about gains before loss control; one bad trade or day can set you back weeks or months.

lessons.title: Tight stops let a small risk carry a large position
lessons.rule: A very close stop lets him put a large share of the account into one stock - 25%, 40%, 45% in his 2021 examples - while risking only a fraction of a percent, and it lets him move the stop to cost much faster. To grow a small account you need big size; to take size without big risk you need a thin stop; to survive a thin stop you need clean setups and exact timing; and to build timing you practise with many small trades.

how.text: Examples: SRF 25% size with a 0.4% stop; HAPPSTMNDS 40% size with a 0.5% stop; GUJGASLTD a 1% stop risking 0.2% made 1.05% on the portfolio from a 6% move.
A smaller stop means higher allocation and a faster move to breakeven (CHAMBALFERT free trade in 4 minutes), after which he feels mentally free.

Adjust the stop % for price: with a 0.05 tick, 1% on a Rs 50 stock is 10 ticks but on a Rs 2,000 stock 400 ticks, so he uses smaller % stops on four-digit stocks and buys more quantity for the same risk.
Size up with a small stop (IRCTC at 0.5%); in a choppy, rotational market he tightens stops and gets out earlier.
He prefers less room and small 'slaps' over wider stops that mean more risk or a smaller bet; a 1:10 trade leaves room for 10 mistakes, 1:18 for 18.
To get there, practise with many small trades first so you survive the learning phase.

lessons.when: On clean setups where a close, logical stop exists.

mistakes.text: Giving the stop more room, which raises risk or forces a smaller bet and lower profitability.
Using the same % stop on a cheap stock as on a high-priced one, which leaves it only a few ticks away.

lessons.evolution: Partly. The 2023 tweet listed size, stop and timing (2023: 1662338937036107776); five weeks later he added practising small to survive the learning phase (2023: 1675414491905794050).

examples.caption: SRF daily bar chart, Aug 2021: after a steep run to ~9,000 the stock moves sideways in a tight range; a green arrow marks his entry near 8,955, where a 0.4% stop let him take 25% size.

CHAMBALFERT daily, July 2021: two months of tight range under ~316 after a May surge, with the last bar breaking to the top of the range - the trade that became risk-free within 4 minutes because the stop was small.

lessons.title: When losses pile up: cut size first, then stop trading
lessons.rule: His account rule: if down 2-3%, cut position size in half; if down another 2%, stop trading for at least a week. An older version (posted Feb 2020, reposted 2022): if 3 of 5 positions hit their stops, take a week off, come back with 50% capital and raise it only once you are making money. The first job in a losing streak is to stop the bleeding by going small; within a single day, he stops adding after the first two positions fail.

how.text: Down 2-3%: halve position size. Down another 2%: suspend trading for at least a week.
2020 rule: 3 of 5 stops hit -> a week off, return with 50% capital, increase only if making money, otherwise repeat.
Go small and cut exposure to stop the bleeding; drop to tiny size even if it is boring. The aim of small size is to regain market feel, not gains.
Daily brake: do not push the envelope on a day the first two positions failed; after the second stop of the day he is done for the day.
He credits these rules with getting him out before large falls, including the Covid crash.

lessons.when: When the account is falling or stops are being hit in succession.

mistakes.text: Fighting back with bigger bets to recover quickly after back-to-back losses.
Refusing to trade your smallest size because it seems pointless - the market will eventually make you small anyway.
Adding trades on a day that started badly.

examples.caption: Screenshot of his 28 Feb 2020 tweet 'No new trades for a week! Time off', quoting his 2018 rule: if 3 of 5 positions hit their stop, take a week off, return with 50% capital and increase only once making money.
Nifty 50 daily, Aug 2019 - Apr 2020: a blue arrow in early March 2020 marks where his rule forced a break, just before the index fell from ~11,300 to ~7,600.

lessons.title: Take a break after stops cluster
lessons.rule: When stops are hit back to back, several in the same week, or a set share of the account is lost, he blames the market and goes on a break - rest of the week, a week, or 7-10 days. Before suspending he may take 2-3 more trades at smaller size; if those fail, he stops. He comes back with small test trades and builds only if the feedback is good, otherwise he extends the break.

how.text: Trigger: many stops in one week is unusual for him, so he blames the market and stops (e.g. 3 trailing stops in a day in 2021; 3 stops in 2 days in Dec 2024).
Before a full stop, 2-3 more trades at smaller size; if they lose too, a week off.
If even the smallest size gets no traction, take 7-10 days off.
Come back with small trades taken for confidence, not money; build if feedback is good, else extend the break. He has cut a break short when open positions (IREDA, PFC) gained.
His insight: whenever the market forced him from 100% invested to 20-25%, trading in the next 5 days almost never made money and usually cost at least 1% more, so he stopped trying.
After breaking his own risk rules in a fall, he says to punish yourself with something like 2-3 weeks of no trades.

lessons.when: After clustered stop-outs or a sharp portfolio drop; he applies it repeatedly in 2024 (March, May, June-July, December).

mistakes.text: Refusing to take a break because you cannot accept not making money every day.
Playing small through difficult conditions instead of learning to sit out - same effort, far lower reward.
Punching trade after trade after many stops hit in one day, which he reads as a change of character.

lessons.title: Size follows feedback, confidence and the environment
lessons.rule: Position size reflects how well his trades are working and how confident he is in the market: small after a break or when trades fail, and pressing the gas fast when recent trades work. Profit from a winning trade becomes the budget for bigger risk on the next ones, so original capital is not exposed. In strong markets he deliberately trades big.

how.text: First trades after a break are for confidence; when COCHINSHIP (a 9 lakh position) worked, the next trade NSLNISP was 28 lakh.
From smallest size to full throttle in under 10 days once trades worked (July 2024); after a month small, he bought 5-10 times that size.
Use gains from the last trade to risk more on the next (TTML -> LICI, BDL); profit from ADANIENT and RCF financed later trades so a run of losers did not hurt.
Size up on a winning streak (double size on ADANIENT's second attempt) - 'because I made money, so risking more'.
Tie exposure to the environment: e.g. status YELLOW -> keep exposure 20-40% for the next 3-4 days and do not open 2-3 trades together; deploy more only on the success of what is already deployed.
When markets are strong, a desk reminder says 'TRADE BIG' and 'MOVE ON'; he does not take a small position just to feel safe.

lessons.when: Whenever deciding how much to put on the next trade.

mistakes.text: Mistaking a low drawdown for skill when you may simply be playing too small.
Letting small size become a comfort zone; under-allocating out of fear rather than because the setup was small.
Getting tempted to size up right after a crash; the environment matters more than the setup.

lessons.evolution: Partly: in 2022 the language is about letting profits finance bigger risk (1536565007835865089); from 2024 he frames size as tracking feedback and confidence (1782707894737138090, 1856190364874338588); in 2026 he adds the warning that trading small can become a comfort zone (2070522482352640425).

examples.caption: Club message: when you come back from a break, the first few trades are not for money but to get the confidence back.

Club update, 24 Mar 2026: environment status kept YELLOW, exposure 20-40% for the next 3-4 days, go slow and don't open 2-3 trades together.

Club note, Dec 2023: learnings from the Sep-Oct crash - don't get tempted right after it, environment matters more than the setup, use the gains and confidence of recent trades to press the gas, and no casual risk management.

lessons.title: Losing streaks: change the size, never the exit rules
lessons.rule: He manages losing streaks with simple count rules: cut size after about 4 losing trades in a row, stop after another 4, and go back to bigger size after 2 wins. When good trades keep coming back to cost, the feedback is to keep going smaller until breakouts work again - not to start taking smaller gains.

how.text: Cut size after ~4 losers in a row, stop after 4 more, return to bigger size after 2 wins.
His spreadsheet tracks the current losing streak (closed trades only) against a threshold he sets between 4 and 10, and flags 'cut size to half' when it is reached.
When breakouts get no follow-through, trade very low size until several good hits come in a row, or until 2-3 big moves are caught.
Oct 2026: JGCHEM, ICIL and BLUESTONE each rose 7-10% and were stopped at cost; he kept his sell rules and adjusted size instead.

lessons.when: During a run of losing or scratched trades.

mistakes.text: Changing sell rules to take smaller gains because a few trades came back.

lessons.evolution: No clear change: shrinking size until trades work appears in 2022 (1551800030020771840) and 2026 (2105520694343913664); the explicit 4/4/2 count is only stated in 2026 (2054140861076967734).

examples.caption: His spreadsheet: losing streak 4 against a streak threshold of 4 (choose 4-10, closed trades only) with the warning 'CUT SIZE TO HALF'; top open positions DATAPATTNS and GROWW.

lessons.title: Outperform by losing little in bad markets
lessons.rule: He says you outperform the market mainly by not losing much in bad times, which is easier than outperforming in an uptrend. One good period is enough to climb out of a drawdown; the rest of the time you control drawdowns and save your ammunition for the easy days.

how.text: 2022: index topped on 18 Jan and fell 20%+; he kept losses small with a per-day limit, avoided overtrading on bad starts, and a few winners put him at a 52-week high. In the April-May 2022 fall of 15% his drawdown from peak was 3.3%.
2024: he stopped on 6 March while the MidSmall index fell 9% from its peak; he was down 4.98%.
A portfolio hit does not matter if you can come back strongly when the right conditions return.
Aim for controlled monthly losses.

lessons.when: During corrections and difficult markets.

mistakes.text: Taking a low drawdown as proof of skill when it may only mean playing too small.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: Nifty Smallcap 100 daily, Oct 2021 - Mar 2022: a green arrow marks the 18 Jan top, after which the index falls from ~12,000 to ~9,300 - the fall through which he kept losses small.
Club message: despite several big drop days since 23 Sep, the portfolio is worth more than then; a hit does not matter if you come back strongly when conditions return.

lessons.title: Size so no gap-down can do lasting damage
lessons.rule: Overnight gaps are handled by position size, not by hope or the stop order. He sizes so a gap could cost at most a few percent of the account, says no gap has ever hit 2% of his portfolio, and only takes home the part of a large intraday position that a gap down could not kill.

how.text: Arithmetic: 10% of capital in a stock that gaps 20% is a 2% portfolio hit; a 10% position with a 2% stop risks 0.2%.

Intraday he may hold over 25%, even 100%+ of the account in one stock, but trims to a comfortable level before taking it home (IEX 35% sold down, BEL 45% sold down, a 25% position cut to 5% for gap risk).
Avoid stocks that mostly move in circuits and trade liquid names that allow an easy exit; he says he has never had a 10% gap-down in his career, nor a 20% one in small caps.
If a stock gaps through the stop, exit at market rather than wait for your price.
He had AI check stocks with Rs 5 crore+ average turnover: 20%+ gap-downs over a year were extremely rare.
Before risk events he cuts size across the whole portfolio by a set percentage instead of cherry-picking (14 Mar and 5 May 2023), or goes slow (FED meeting).
In a crisis, zero or light exposure is the ultimate protection.

lessons.when: Every day a position is carried overnight, and before known events.

mistakes.text: Worrying about last night's DOW fall or spending the weekend glued to news - a sign you were oversized.
Fearing a 20% gap while holding a losing stock for years, which is the bigger risk.
Waiting for your stop price after a gap instead of exiting at market.
