modules.title: Managing open trades
modules.intro: Once a trade is on, Manas reduces risk as fast as the stock allows - stop to cost at around 2R, sometimes a slice sold - then adds to what is working and leaves it alone through squats and scary candles. Trades that do not move the way his winners do are cut early, the add lot first. He manages on the daily close rather than the live tape, has a specific routine for panic-day opens, and watches settlement holidays and the tax side of exits.

lessons.title: Make it risk-free fast: stop to cost
lessons.rule: Once a trade moves about 2R in his favour he raises the stop to his entry - a 'free trade' - so from then on he either makes a good amount or loses nothing. Often he pairs it with selling a first slice. He calls himself a risk manager first: as soon as a trade moves, he reduces its risk, which frees his mind and creates room for new trades. Breakeven exits are accepted as the cost.

how.text: At about 2R, move the stop to cost (GRAPHITE, KOTAKBANK, ABB, CDSL, GNFC in 2021); tight stops make this happen within minutes.

Later examples at 2-5R or after a sharp move: MRPL at 4R, GUJALKALI at 5R, CREDITACC, ELGIEQUIP, CANBK, NIFTY futures, RCF, J_KBANK, IRFC, HEMIPROP (11% intraday), GOLDIAM (+16%), INOXWIND, HBLENGINE, AMBER, GROWW, GRAPHITE (7R), WALCHANNAG, EXICOM, SUVEN, ICIL.

Often sell about a third into the first strength and trail the rest with the stop at cost (BAJFINANCE 1/3 at 3R, RAIN, ENGINERSIN; NFL 25%, TEXRAIL, JBMA) to make space for more trades without stressing the portfolio.
Partial steps are fine too: TEXRAIL stop raised from 2% to 1% after a 3% move; PRIVISCL stop cut from -1R to -0.4R - defensive on capital, aggressive by leaving the upside open.
Being a risk manager first keeps him mentally free and lets him take the next trade; one or two of them end up doing really well.

lessons.when: As soon as a new position moves clearly in his favour.

mistakes.text: Letting a breakeven exit hurt; when three trades that were up 7-10% were stopped at cost he kept the rule and moved on.

lessons.evolution: No clear change: the same stop-to-cost habit runs from 2021 (1379676213518553088) to 2026 (2090333404718059564); from 2025 he adds that the purpose is to make room for more trades (1929764798608109825).

examples.caption: ABB daily, Mar-Apr 2021: a green arrow marks the entry bar off the April low near 1,310; within the session it reached 1,360, already 2R, and he moved the stop to cost.
Club note, Apr 2024: HUDCO faded on day 0 while JAMNAAUTO rose, then HUDCO was up 9% the next day - 'stop overthinking, give your trades time and leave them alone'.

lessons.title: Pyramid into what is working
lessons.rule: Most people think about selling; he thinks about how to add more. He starts with a starter position, gives it a day or two of feedback, and adds 2nd, 3rd and more entries only while it works - each add treated as a fresh entry ('if this were my first buy, would I buy here?'). Raising the stop on earlier buys as he adds keeps the combined risk from growing, so gains on the first buys finance the later ones. An add that does not stick is closed on its own the same or next day, and the original keeps running.

how.text: Feedback first: give the first buys a day or two to say whether to add or cut to zero.
Add after the pullback is done and it breaks out again, near or slightly above the base breakout - not once the stock is already 25-30% above the base.
Each add must be a valid fresh entry on its own: forget the first entry and ask whether you would buy here today.

Raise the stop on earlier lots as you add so total risk does not rise (ASAHIINDIA: stop to 575 made the first three buys risk-free and financed the 4th, later the 5th; DIXON first entry risk-free 'made room' for the 2nd; RPOWER: increase size without adding portfolio risk).
Close the add's quantity alone if it fails ('Closed today's buy': AFFLE, ASAHIINDIA, AVTNPL, GUJALKALI, EICHERMOT, EASEMYTRIP, HSCL, CAMPUS, ANGELONE, JSWINFRA, IRB, MARKSANS, DLF).
Given a choice between a new name and more of an existing winner, he always adds to the existing one; later adds can even be larger than the first ('when you know your game, break all the rules').

Campaigns he posted: PCJEWELLER four buys from 15.5 to 30; ADANIENT bought at 2314 and added on the way up to 3,700 shares; ZENTEC six or more adds; NCC 7th add; COCHINSHIP four entries to 6,925; IRB to 160,200; MOTILALOFS four adds; RAIN four entries; GPIL to his largest position.

lessons.when: On positions that have already given positive feedback, during strong markets.

mistakes.text: Pressing too hard: he admitted to 'pressing the gas a little too hard' on the 4th ASAHIINDIA add.
Pyramiding raises exposure if the trade then fails: THERMAX after three buys ended at a 1.8% portfolio loss.
Thinking only about selling instead of how to add more.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in method: 'buy what you already own, on the way up' (2022: 1557592887025893377); the base-level and feedback rules spelled out (2023: 1665616402798059521); the 'valid fresh entry' question (2025: 2001191793548009762; 2026: 2098272646261817620).

examples.caption: ASAHIINDIA daily, Aug 2022: green arrows mark successive buys from the ~539 low to ~580, and the stock closes at a new high of 620 - the day he raised the stop to 575, making the first three buys risk-free and financing the 4th.
PCJEWELLER weekly, Sep 2020 - Mar 2021: a big December breakout from ~15 followed by higher consolidations along a rising average to ~30 - the stock he bought four times (15.5, 18.5, 26, 30).
His reply on when to add: forget what you are already holding; ask if this was your first buy, would you buy here - if yes, go ahead.

lessons.title: Don't interfere with working trades
lessons.rule: In a trending market, once a trade is on and the stop is set, he leaves it alone. Some trades will fall back and stop him out, but not interfering is what lands the few 50-100R trades a year that take him months ahead; interfering to save open gains costs him that edge. He also does not dump an open position just because another stock is setting up.

how.text: Keep the stop and move away for a few days; let the trade be.
Accept that a trade may go back to his price tomorrow; he holds because interfering loses the edge (ELECTCAST, NSLNISP, YESBANK).
Even with 109,000 TTML shares 12 points off the high and his stop likely to be hit, he did not close early - saving a little now costs far more later.
Don't close good positions because of market fear: you only know the market is bad after it has gone bad (GRAPHITE survived and made a new high).
Don't swap a holding for a new setup; the new one may stall too and the urge never ends.
Detach from the money - want it and not want it at the same time; decide the most you will risk, then let things happen (ZENTEC: 100% in under 16 weeks by not interfering).

lessons.when: On working positions in a trending market; in 2022-type conditions he closed weak trades quickly (see trade_management-8).

mistakes.text: Interfering because the 5-minute chart is 'screaming sell'.
Fear of scary-looking candles on the way to a 100R trade.

examples.caption: Member's message: his first 50% trade came from sitting out and not interfering, after years of squaring off on every dip and watching the stock fly.
Meme 'Aapne ghabrana nahi hai' (you don't have to panic) posted with his line that the road to 100R trades is full of scary candles.

lessons.title: Judge on the daily close; stay off the live tape and the index
lessons.rule: A day that closes strongly bullish can be horribly volatile intraday, so he stresses staying away from the live action: sitting at the screen means being faked out every minute. He removed every index from his screen, places orders in advance and walks away, and lets how a stock closes the day decide what to do with the rest.

how.text: Try not looking at the price before the close of the day as a test of how strong you are.
Remove every index from your screen - try it for two weeks; if you don't trade the index, don't watch it. He says he does not know where Nifty and Sensex are.
Place your orders (bids, stops) in advance and move away from the screen; use alerts sparingly because screen time kills trades.
Use the close as the verdict: how it closes the day decides the remaining position.
He holds overnight rather than trading intraday, citing data that overnight returns beat intraday ones.

lessons.when: Every trading day.

mistakes.text: Sitting on the screen all day and getting faked out.
Panic-closing positions because the index is falling (followers reported fewer panic exits after removing the index).

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: 20 MICRONS daily close-up: a large bullish candle (marked with a pointing hand) after a small red bar - the strong close.
20 MICRONS 5-minute chart of the same session: sharp spikes and slides drawn with orange lines from 9:35 to 13:00 before the late surge - the intraday noise behind that strong daily candle.

lessons.title: Panic-day stop execution: 9:18, then the day's low
lessons.rule: On a panic sell day he does not fire stops in the opening minutes. His action plan: execute stop losses at 9:18; if the day turns into an oops reversal, shift the stop to below the low of the day. It applies only on panic sell days and only for the first few minutes, and he says it has saved many positions from exiting at the worst possible price.

how.text: Execute stops at 9:18 rather than at the open; if an oops reversal develops, move the stop to below the day's low.
Only on panic sell days, only for the first few minutes - otherwise the stop stays in the system.
Examples: GRAPHITE opened weak on 2 Mar 2026 and recovered; the 19 Mar oops reversal 'worked again'; on 11 Sep 2026 the NIFTY long would otherwise have been sold near the day's low.
When a gap opens below his stop, the stop for the day becomes a little below the day's low, and if there is no decent recovery by the close he exits rather than carry more gap risk.
Panic-day plan also includes no new trades for a few days and a review in 3 days.

lessons.when: Only on panic sell-off opens.

mistakes.text: Using it while oversized: if you cannot afford to wait to 9:18 you deserve the punishment; he accepts it can go wrong on a Covid-type day and judges it over ~1,000 trades.

lessons.evolution: No clear change; all tweets are from March-September 2026.

examples.caption: Club action plan with the key line boxed: execute stop losses at 9:18; if it turns into an oops reversal day, shift the stop to below the low of the day; no new trades for the next few days, review in 3 days.
GRAPHITE daily, 2 Mar 2026: after a red bar from ~730, the boxed day opens weak near 685 and climbs to ~714 by mid-morning - the position the 9:18 rule kept.

lessons.title: Sit through squats and pullbacks to catch 20-50R
lessons.rule: Big winners squat, pull back and give up open profit on the way. If you cannot sit through squats, pullbacks and loss of open gains - or are not ready to risk 6-7% of open gain - he says you will never catch a 25R trade or a 40% move. Most of the shaking happens in the early part of a move; then buyers take control and the ride smooths out.

how.text: Expect to watch a sized stock go 188 -> 215 -> 195 -> 225 and behave as if nothing happened (AEQUS). Your stock can be volatile; you don't have to be.
Give 6-7% of room on open gains if you want the 40% moves.
Most shakeouts come in the early 'gears' of a move; later the stock gives its final explosive leg (PaisaLo, AEQUS).
Big winners do not act well every day - study them before demanding that of your position.
Accept that only 2-3 trades become big winners.

lessons.when: On positions that are working but pausing.

mistakes.text: Taking 1-2R and sitting in front of the screen all day instead of sitting through squats.
Expecting big moves without risking open gains - unrealistic expectations.

lessons.evolution: No clear change; the explicit 25R / 6-7% statements are from 2026 (2049405017883652271, 2074730351663169728).

examples.caption: AEQUS daily at his June 2026 entry: after an April-May run from ~125 to ~220 the stock pulled back below a now-falling average; the entry marker sits near 188 - the position that later went 188 -> 215 -> 195 -> 225.

lessons.title: Winners work fast: cut what struggles
lessons.rule: From tracking his trades he knows his winners don't take long to work, and if they do take long they usually don't work. So he cuts trades that stall, close weak or show no buying interest - often within hours or a day or two - instead of waiting for the stop. In 2025 he put it as: no strong follow-up within T+3 days and a trade is likely to hit its stop. That keeps his average loser below 1R.

how.text: Time stops in 2021-2023: no movement or thrust for 1-3 hours = out ('my wins don't take this long').
Taking longer than his average winning time: reduce, then close (NYKAA, MANAPPURAM, ASTRAL, LICI, INDIACEM, AMBUJACEM sold 80% at a snail's pace).
Out on a weak or dull close the same day (SOBHA, DEVYANI, TATAPOWER, PARAS, KPITTECH), or after a day of no buying interest (ANGELONE).
'My winners don't usually struggle a lot' - reduce risk when they do (GNFC vs CAMPUS); ruthlessly close struggling breakouts.
2025: if no strong follow-up within T+3 days, the trade is likely to hit its stop - one of the rules that had him at zero holdings before the April 2025 fall.

2026: NETWEB closed half at entry and the rest at the stop - a 0.4% hit on a Rs 92 lakh position instead of 1%; his journal shows avg winner 6.12R vs avg loser 0.79R. Knowing a bad position before the stop comes only from experience of how winners behave.
Exception: the 'too long to work' exit does not apply to shorts at a top, which take time to crack.

lessons.when: In the first hours and days of a new position.

mistakes.text: Hoping or praying on a bad position instead of getting out and finding the next winner.
Demanding that a large position act well every day; he notes big winners don't.

examples.caption: AI-built journal summary of 20 trade ideas: average winner 6.12R, average loser 0.79R, win/loss ratio 7.8x; best setup 'Hold 4-7 days' with a profit factor of 12.49.
Broker fills for NETWEB: two lots of 675 shares sold at 3,409.02 and 3,409.04 - the half closed at entry when the trade didn't work fast.

lessons.title: Operational frictions: settlement holidays and the intraday tax adjustment
lessons.rule: Two practical points he flags. Around trading and settlement holidays a stock bought cannot be sold for days, so in a gap-down market he avoids opening trades just before such breaks; selling the day after buying also carries short-delivery risk. On the tax side, intraday losses cannot be set off against delivery gains, so when a new position gains well on its entry day he closes it and immediately rebuys to book an intraday gain against carried-forward intraday losses.

how.text: 31 Mar trading holiday + 1 Apr settlement holiday meant a Monday 30 March buy could only be sold on 2 April, so he advised against opening trades that Monday.
He could not exit J&KBANK on a settlement holiday and held it with a prior-day-low stop instead.
Selling the next day risks short delivery, and the broker has no role in it.
Tax adjustment: lock an entry-day intraday gain by selling and rebuying at once (AEQUS, STALLION); intraday losses can be carried forward 4 years against intraday gains only.

lessons.when: Before trading/settlement holidays and on the entry day of a position that gains well.

mistakes.text: Selling shares bought the previous day without knowing about short delivery - you find out only after a hard hit.

lessons.evolution: No clear change; tweets are from 2026 (the tax note image is dated Dec 2024).

examples.caption: Club note: 31 Mar trading holiday and 1 Apr settlement holiday mean stock bought on Monday 30 March can only be sold on 2 April - in a gap-down market, no sense opening trades on Monday.

Club 'Tax tip' (3 Dec 2024): intraday losses cannot be set off against delivery gains but can be carried forward 4 years against intraday gains; a good entry-day gain can be locked by closing and reopening immediately.

modules.title: Selling
modules.intro: Manas sells for two reasons only: the stop or trailing stop is hit, or the stock gets super extended and he sells part of it into strength. He sets no price targets, scales out in pieces at multiples of risk, trails the rest, and keeps swing expectations realistic - he puts the typical upper end of an Indian swing at roughly 40-60%, so he takes the 'fat middle' rather than waiting for the top. Separately, he exits positions that have no profit cushion before a gap risk such as an overnight hold, a weekend or results.

lessons.title: Sell into strength in pieces; take the fat middle
lessons.rule: He books profit as the stock rises rather than waiting for weakness, selling in pieces at multiples of risk and riding the remainder. In 2021 he described it as half between 3-5R, more at 7-10R, and the last part trailed. Because a swing trade has an upper limit - he puts it at about 40-45% (2021), about 50% with most names not passing 30% (2025), and 50-60% as the bread and butter (2026) - if you don't sell into strength near that limit, you end up selling into weakness later.

how.text: Scale out at R multiples: half or a third at 3-5R, more at 7-10R, trail the last part with whichever of the 5 or 10 MA the stock respects. Play for the majority; only a few become monster winners.
Typical trades: first sale of 20-50% (TWL 20%, GUJALKALI 20% at ~3R, IREDA 20% at 28R then 30% at 31.5R, EPACK 50% at +30% then 40% at +38%), with the rest held.

Sell larger pieces when the move looks stretched or accelerates (NTPC large part at 22R, ADANIENT majority on an extended gap-up then more at 10.5-26R, fully out at 30R after a month, IRFC 50% when 'very stretched', NLCINDIA 40% when extended a second time).

Expectation setting: swing moves average 20-40% (2021); about 50% with most below 30% (2025); 50-60% is the bread and butter, and he closed FCL's last part after a 50% swing, 'the upper end' in India (2026).
Selling into strength keeps the equity curve smooth instead of a roller coaster, and it lets profits compound.
Recent scale-outs at 5-7R with the rest riding (NETWEB 1/3 at 7R then held to 34R; DATAPATTNS 5R and 6R; DELTACORP 5R; MIDHANI 6R).

lessons.when: When a winner is up several R, extended, or near the typical upper limit of a swing.

mistakes.text: Holding the full position for the top; the stock will force you to sell into weakness days or weeks later.
Not having clear objective rules for booking profit, which he calls ten times harder than buying.

lessons.evolution: His stated upper limit for a swing rises over time: 20-40% average / 40-45% 'moon' (2021: 1355134072096317447), about 50% with most below 30% (2025: 1962818192214237607), 50-60% bread and butter (2026: 2056627373475524929).

examples.caption: GMDC daily, May 2026: after a base capped around 639 since October, a single +20% bar breaks out to 746; his note reads 'I'd sell majority here if I were holding it' - the stock was already up 47%.

His Aug 2025 post: swing trading has an upper limit of about 50% on average, most names don't cross 30%, so start selling partially into strength near the limit rather than holding the full position for the top.
IRFC daily, Dec 2023: a green arrow at the breakout near 77, then a near-vertical run to 95.65 on heavy volume - where he closed 50% because it looked very stretched.

lessons.title: No price targets: the trailing stop decides the final exit
lessons.rule: He has no targets - 'God and a liar can give you a target' is his line - because nobody knows how far a stock will go. Stocks can go much higher than imagined (ZENTEC 4.5x in 6 months), so capping the upside with targets costs the trades that take you months ahead. The remaining position goes when the trailing stop is hit or the stock stops behaving.

how.text: Do not answer 'what is the target'; take the breakout from a tight zone with no idea how far it will go.
Don't cap the upside; move beyond 1:3 (GRAPHITE held to 14R).
Asked for his selling rule, his answer was 'Don't sell.'

Final exits come from the trailing stop or the stock not acting right: COCHINSHIP trailing stop hit at 1233 from 1057; EMUDHRA closed at its stop at 475 after reaching 534; SJVN remainder at ~89; JSWENERGY closed because it didn't stick.
Use alerts sparingly: alerts pull you to the screen, and screen time kills the trade (a trader with alerts at 5-7R never caught 10-15R moves). Place orders in advance and move away.
Accept the trade-off: trailing with a moving average will sometimes give back gains, but it removes stress and catches gigantic moves.

lessons.when: For the final part of every winning position.

mistakes.text: Wanting big gains while refusing to risk open gains - you end up moving in circles.
Being stopped out and then complaining that the stock ran; he had 44,000 APOLLO stopped at 67 before it went to 91.4 and simply moved on.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: COCHINSHIP daily, Sep-Dec 2023: green arrows mark his entry and adds around 1,050-1,100 in November; the stock runs to ~1,330, and on 20 Dec a wide red bar drops to ~1,265 - his trailing stop was hit and the whole position closed at 1233.

lessons.title: The most bullish bar late in a rally is large money getting out
lessons.rule: A huge-volume, widest up bar that arrives late in a long advance often marks institutions exiting, not a breakout. After it the upside tends to be limited, with false breakouts, until the stock goes through a meaningful correction. He addressed this to positional and buy-and-hold holders, not to traders playing 2-5% moves.

how.text: Look for the most bullish bar on huge volume after the stock is already up a lot.
Examples he posted: BAJAJAUTO, RELIANCE, AARTIDRUGS, IOLCP, AUROPHARMA; he sold GLENMARK on its volume climax and it went sideways after.
He expected the pharma names with the steepest rise to fall hardest (50-80% from the high); IOLCP was 40% down from its top a month later.
A bullish broker rating on a stock already up 5x was followed by TATAMOTORS' largest down bar of the move.
After such a bar, don't expect big moves unless the stock first corrects meaningfully (ideally ~50%).

lessons.when: When a long-held stock prints its biggest volume bar late in an extended run.

mistakes.text: Reading that bar as a fresh breakout to buy; day traders and 4-5% players can ignore this signal.

lessons.evolution: No clear change; the examples are from Jan-Jul 2021.

examples.caption: BAJAJ_AUTO daily, Jan-Feb 2021: green arrows mark a huge-volume, wide up bar to ~4,100; the stock then stalls for weeks and slides to ~3,900.
BAJAJ_AUTO weekly, 2020 - Jan 2021: after a long recovery from the Covid low, the latest week is the largest up bar on the largest volume of the chart - the bar he called large money getting out.

lessons.title: Don't cut winners at 3-10%
lessons.rule: Booking at 3-4% or after a 4% move feels safe but wastes the rally and kills the trades that grow the account; the bad phase will take away more. Solving the '5% problem' by closing at 5% means never seeing 10, 20 or 30%. Change the question from where to take profits to how to buy more.

how.text: Hold through the dips that come after a 5% gain; many of those trades go to 10, 20, 30%.
Obsess over the process and clear rules, not over money - booking every little gain out of fear keeps money away.
To win big, consciously play for it: sit on trades with size for a bigger % move, and think about adding rather than selling early.
Don't trade a good swing entry with an intraday mindset: a NEWGEN reversal entry he advised holding went up 40% in 3 days.
A follower averaging 3.27% per trade with 80% same-day exits was effectively a day trader while stocks rose 30-80%; either churn more trades or sit longer on a few.

lessons.when: In the early part of a winning trade, when the urge to bank a small gain is strongest.

mistakes.text: Booking at 10% and then feeling stupid when the stock goes to 20%.
Taking profit after a 4% move because it avoids pain.
Regret thinking - 'I should have closed' - which he says ends trading careers.

lessons.evolution: No clear change: the message appears in 2023 (1645992675882029057) and 2026 (2067615820914557080).

examples.caption: Member-club thread, 17 Feb 2026: a member posts 'Long in NewGen @ 471, Intraday'; Manas replies the trade is fine but not to take it with an intraday mindset.

lessons.title: Only two reasons to sell: the stop, or super extended
lessons.rule: 'Sell when it hits your stop or when it gets super extended' - he says this solves most selling problems and there is no third scenario. The extended exit is discretionary: when a stock rises at a 70-90 degree angle it often kills the momentum for days, so he sells at market rather than trail. For traders who hate watching big open gains vanish, he offers staggered stops as the alternative.

how.text: Exit 1: the stop or trailing stop is hit. Pick your own level; there is no perfectly safe level.

Exit 2: super extended - sell at market when the angle of rise goes to roughly 70-90 degrees, because such a rise usually stalls for days and he prefers to scale out rather than hold a stagnant position (e.g. OLECTRA).
When a stock rises too fast to trail, he takes it all (RCF: 20R in 3 days, fully out); a pop in an already extended stock usually kills the trend for weeks (BECTORFOOD closed).
If losing open gains hurts you more than selling early, use staggered stops: bought at 100, now 115 - put half the stop at 107.5 and half at 100; the 50% split can be 35-60%.

lessons.when: Every day a position is open.

mistakes.text: Wanting both - big moves and no give-back of open gains - which keeps you going in circles.
Choosing the staggered stop and then complaining when the stock runs from 107.5 to 130 without you.

examples.caption: COCHINSHIP daily, Apr 2024: entry arrow near 880 after a shakeout, then a near-vertical 25-30% run to ~1,135 within days - where he sold part into strength at 1129.5.
BECTORFOOD daily, May 2023: entry arrow around 649, then a +9.6% pop on heavy volume to 722 in an already extended stock - he closed the whole position.

lessons.title: Trail the rest with a moving average - shorter when extended
lessons.rule: For the part left after selling into strength he trails the stop with a moving average: typically the 20-period, and a 10- or even 5-period when the trend is exceptionally strong and extended (2023); in 2021 he described trailing the last portion on whichever of the 5 or 10 MA the stock respected most. By 2025-26 he trails with what he calls an 'E stop' set under recent price structure rather than a strict MA stop, because stocks often use their MAs as add points, not exits.

how.text: Default trail: 20-period MA; tighten to the 10 or 5 when the trend is exceptionally strong and extended.
Last portion: the 5 or 10 MA, whichever the stock has respected most.
After a new high he may raise the stop to that day's low (RELINFRA).

E stop (2025-26 ChartGym examples): most traders keep a strict stop at the MA and get closed out; he watches what the stock does around the MA, where pullbacks often become add points, and raises the stop under structure (NAVINFLUOR 'New E stop', GESHIP 'SL hit').
After a trailing exit, nothing may happen for months (BSOFT: two months of nothing after the exit), which he uses as validation.
Accept that trailing gives some gains back; that is the price of catching the big moves.

lessons.when: On the remaining position after partial sales, for as long as the trend lasts.

mistakes.text: Keeping a strict stop exactly at the MA and closing trades that were only using it as support.

lessons.evolution: Shift in method: an MA trail - 5/10 MA (2021: 1448542456362909696), 20-period tightened to 10/5 (2023: 1665293414210891777) - then an 'E stop' that treats MA touches as possible add points rather than exits (2026: 2030619663768723652).

examples.caption: ChartGym slide (NAVINFLUOR daily): a dashed 'New E stop' raised under the latest breakout bar; note says he trails with an E stop because most traders keep strict MA stops, while he watches how stocks act around MAs, which often become add points.
ChartGym slide (GESHIP daily): after a steady run above its rising averages, a red bar breaks the dashed stop line - labelled 'SL hit'.
BSOFT daily: a long trend above its MAs rolls over into a sideways range; a ruler marks 38 bars with the note 'Nothing happened next 2 months' after the exit.

lessons.title: Don't take profits at old resistance lines
lessons.rule: Staring at the resistance ahead makes traders cut winners; managing the trade on what price is doing now lets a winner run through old levels. He showed RVNL with four old highs marked as resistance and, the same day, the stock having sliced through all of them.

how.text: Manage the trade on current price action rather than lines from old highs.
He reframes strength: instead of looking for a place to take profits, look for a place to add.

lessons.when: When a winner approaches an old high.

mistakes.text: Drawing lines and taking profits at them instead of letting the winner run.

examples.caption: RVNL daily, Sep 2021 - Sep 2022, with dashed red resistance lines at 34.00, 37.40, 39.30 and 44.80 drawn from old highs.
The same RVNL chart extended to Nov 2022: price breaks through all four lines and runs vertically to 59.50.

lessons.title: No profit cushion, no gap risk: exit before overnight, weekends and results
lessons.rule: If a fresh position has not built a profit cushion, he closes it rather than carry it into a gap risk - overnight, a long weekend, or a results announcement. With a cushion he may hold or only trim. He also sells part in pre-market when he expects a bad open, and steps back when the index itself is extended.

how.text: Close a new position at day end if it has no cushion (MEGH, MTARTECH, CDSL, IEX, ASTRAZEN in 2021; TATAMOTORS, TATASTEEL, NFL, VTL, ADANIENT in 2022).
Long weekends need a bigger cushion (TATASTEEL closed at 1.3R before a long weekend; BAJAJAUTO with a 0.5% stop closed before a weekend).
Trim to a size he is comfortable holding overnight (RADICO), or sell half pre-market before an expected bad open (HINDOILEXP).

Results: keep a strict stop or lock half on the day (IIFL, PRINCEPIPE); close when there is no cushion (NAVA, OIL, DCAL, PRIVISCL closed at 2560); with momentum fading and results due, exit fully (SDBL).
When results gap a stock through the stop, get out at the open rather than wait for the stop price (DCAL).
He insists this is not day trading: the intention is to hold, and the exit happens only when the cushion is missing.

lessons.when: Near the close on entry day, before weekends/holidays, and on results days.

mistakes.text: Entering on a results day without noticing (BDL, 2023 - 'my bad').

examples.caption: Trade-book line for VTL, June 2022: 4,100 shares bought at 264.94 and the same 4,100 sold at 265.31 the same day - a scratch exit because there was no profit cushion to hold overnight.

modules.title: Psychology
modules.intro: He treats behaviour, not technique, as the hard part: sitting out bad markets, accepting stop-outs that later run, treating losses as a business cost, and overcoming the fear of giving back open profit.

lessons.title: The Power of Sitting Out: Extreme Patience During Hostile Markets
lessons.rule: Not trading is a position. Sitting out a bad phase preserves gains that took months to make, and his stated edge is waiting for the right time and showing up hard when it comes.

how.text: He watches down days 'from the outside' and counts sitting them out as a win.
Switching off is a skill, harder to hone than trading.
Protection mode after a good month: hold only a minuscule position and preserve what was made.
Long stretches in full cash when conditions are wrong: zero holdings and terminal off (Apr 2025), 100% cash (Jun and Aug 2025), no trades through Nov-Dec 2025.
His edge is identifying the right time and patiently waiting for it; he makes alpha by not losing in bad markets.
Cut the news noise in crises; constant headlines add stress without improving decisions.

lessons.when: Corrections, choppy tapes and around big events.

mistakes.text: Playing small in difficult conditions instead of learning to sit out.
Needing trading income, which takes away the luxury of sitting out.
Itchy fingers giving back gains; you are your own biggest enemy.

lessons.evolution: 2021-2022 he often played smaller in hard conditions (1438720843278811137, 1442744734825385984); Jan 2024 he said playing small costs you the skill of sitting out and gives low reward for the same effort (1744326324892910041).

examples.caption: Index table, 23 Sep 2022: Bank Nifty -2.93%, Nifty -1.86%, Midsmall -2.13%, Smallcap -2.10%, the fall he sat out.

lessons.title: Regret Management: Accept Being Stopped Out Right Before the Move
lessons.rule: Being stopped out just before a stock flies happens to him constantly, even after years. Take ownership of the stop you chose, accept it as part of the business, and find the next trade.

how.text: APOLLO: 44,000 shares at about 63, ran to 74, stopped at 67 in a bad environment, then locked at a 20% upper circuit at 91.4. He took a deep breath and moved on: not the first, not the last.
There is no escape from it; his equity curve has countless such trades and it does not matter in the grand scheme.
Manage it by moving on to the next trade, the next APOLLO.
Own the decision: if you chose a 2% stop and got chopped out, the stock did not tell you to.
A shakeout followed by reversal is normal behaviour; buy it again sometime in the coming days if it sets up.
Squats and stop-outs happen even in the best markets; the problem is expecting every trade to be a superhero.

lessons.when: After a stop-out that is followed by a big move.

mistakes.text: Widening stops to avoid it; that creates the need for much bigger moves.
Blaming the market or crying over the decision you made.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: APOLLO MICRO daily to 31 Oct 2023: two green arrows near 60-63 in early October, a late-month pullback, then a 19.95% candle to 91.40 on heavy volume.
His equity curve, rising over time with flat and dipping stretches, shared with the note that it holds countless trades that stopped him and then ran.

lessons.title: Move On Immediately: Embrace Bad Days and Never Carry Baggage
lessons.rule: The market will keep throwing bad days, scratches and breakeven exits. Use them to build strength, trade the present rather than the past, and never let an old loss block the next trade.

how.text: Use bad days to build yourself stronger; the market will throw such days your whole trading life, so you cannot afford to lose mentally on them.
Moving on means a portfolio hit does not matter if you come back strongly when the right conditions return.
Your old loss is blocking your next big trade.
After a breakeven exit or a gain that went to cost: 'grab your balls and move on', find the next one.
Trade the now, not your past.
When open gains evaporate, read it as the market not ready yet; save the account and go heavy when the tide turns.
He shows his own mistakes (an INDIGO shakeout, a 20 lakh error) as part of the game.

lessons.when: After a cluster of stops, a scratch, or a painful give-back.

mistakes.text: Letting the last loss block the next trade.
Reacting to a give-back with instant regret about not locking gains.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: Channel messages: use these days to build yourself stronger, the market will keep throwing them, embrace them and move on; then 'Jo aaj hara, woh hamesha harega'.
Channel message: several big drop days since Sep 2023, yet portfolio value is above that level; a hit does not matter if you come back in the right conditions.

lessons.title: Conquer the Fear of Giving Back Open Gains (Alter Ego Technique & Screen Logouts)
lessons.rule: The main reason most traders do not make money is fear, especially of giving back open profit, which makes them sell winners early. He counters it by detaching from the money, staying off the screen, and the Alter Ego idea a club member brought in.

how.text: 90% are scared to give back open gains, and that is why 90% do not make money; he says he was too.
Large R trades are only possible if you detach from the money: do not calculate what you are making mid-trade; counting open gains works against you.
Alter Ego: think and behave like the trader you want to become. A member who cut gains early adopted it, held his trades, and logged out of his trading account when the urge to book came.
Staying off the screen is a deliberate part of the job; he steps away consciously to avoid the urge to take profits.
Profitable trades test you more than losers; your stock can be volatile without you being volatile.
The cost of always locking small gains is losing out on the huge ones.
Make rules from your own pain points, e.g. protect a 10% gain if seeing it go to zero hurts more than missing a run to 50%.
Take the next few trades only to work on fear.

lessons.when: While sitting on open profit in a working trade.

mistakes.text: Counting open gains during the trade.
Checking open positions 10-50 times a day.
Booking every small gain out of fear it will fade.

lessons.evolution: 2021: detach from the money (1470710248507789316); Jul 2024: the Alter Ego idea shared (1809872994199552242); otherwise no clear change in the tweets.

examples.caption: Summary sheet 'Insights from The Alter Ego Effect' by Todd Herman: where/what/who/why steps to build an alter ego, then test and trigger it.
The member's message: holding all trades, they started moving after three days; when the urge to book comes he switches to his office screen and logs out of the trading account.

lessons.title: Behaviour Trumps Technique: The Daily Mindset Checklist and Execution Discipline
lessons.rule: Finding stocks can be learned in days; the right behaviour takes years, and the market rewards in proportion to it. He needs below-average technical skill and stellar mental stability, and keeps written reminders and routines to build it.

how.text: Markets reward in proportion to behaviour; finding stocks is no rocket science, the right behaviour takes years.
Anyone can learn SVRO or VCP; you win only by controlling behaviour. Build mental toughness instead of staring at charts.
His eight-point mental framework, posted daily in his channel: process includes sitting on open profit, nobody knows anything, risk manager first, know your open risk, no fear of missing out.
If still struggling after a year or two, you need to be a better person, not a better system; a stop loss is a promise to yourself.
Write the behavioural issue and its solution down and read it daily for 30 days; keep a mistake sheet and read it weekly.
About 10 minutes most evenings of action replay on past trades to build confidence that the strategy works.
Journal every trade and the mental issues; track performance to the T.
Read Trading in the Zone every few weeks; for fear of losing, Best Loser Wins.
Obsess over the process and clear rules, not money.

lessons.when: Daily, before and after the session.

mistakes.text: Burning the midnight oil on charts while ignoring behaviour.
Looking for a better system after a year or two of struggle.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets; the eight-point framework was posted in Jul 2025 (1950826594106232892).

examples.caption: His channel post 'I will post this every day': eight points including following the process of sitting on open profits, risk manager first, know my open risk, no FOMO, and a handful of good trades taking him far.

lessons.title: Accept 7 Losers in 10: Unemotional Loss-Cutting and Surviving the Early Years
lessons.rule: Prepare for 7 losers in 10, leave the other 3 alone, and accept they can come in any order. Losses are the cost of doing business; cut them without thinking twice so there are no big ones, and survive the early years.

how.text: Prepare for 7 losers out of 10, leave the 3 alone, and show up for all 10; cherry-picking loses the casino's edge.
He calls losses the cost of doing business and posts them that way (e.g. 'portfolio down 0.1%'); the wording took the sting out.
Taking a loss is the easiest part.
Cut any losing position without thinking twice; small losses are normal, big losses are not.
You have to kiss many frogs; a 30% win rate still makes money over the year.
Track 100-150 trades to learn your own mix of instant failures, round trips, small and big winners.
First year: make preserving capital the goal; being near starting capital is doing great.
Have a separate source of income while learning; he sold his car in his early days and struggled for years while depending on trading.
He shares followers' stories that stopping derivatives is what made them profitable, and prefers swing cash trades.

lessons.when: On every stop-out and throughout the early years.

mistakes.text: Expecting every trade to be a hero and to give instant feedback.
Letting a small loss snowball into a big one.
Expecting to be rich within a year.

lessons.evolution: 2021-2023: losses framed as the cost of doing business (1478641836411351042, 1671451798731620352); 2026: stated as building 7 losers in 10 into expectations (2074796997744406829).

examples.caption: His 2018 tweet closing CGCL: 'Total cost of doing business: 1R or 1% of portfolio'.
WhatsApp exchange about a Paytm loss: his advice to move the money to a better stock, with the friend changing from 'keep it' to 'move now'.

modules.title: Tools and routines
modules.intro: His working tools and routines: a trade journal mined for his own statistics, chart study of past winners, a few chart and screen habits, the Purple Dot marker he released free on TradingView, watchlists prepared out of hours, practical order and data checks, the scans that feed his list, and the weekly ChartGym exercise.

lessons.title: Journal Every Trade and Mine Your Own Data
lessons.rule: Write down every trade without delay and study the record. He calls the journal the best trading book you will ever read: it shows what is not working so you can stop repeating it, and it reveals how your own winners and losers behave. He mines it by hand, and from 2025 with AI.

how.text: Write down every single trade with no delay, and note the mental issues too; what gets measured gets managed.
Review your own trades; he says the turning point for every trader he taught came after reviewing them.

Example he shared: a student's review of his first 50 trades showed winners worked within the first week or two and every trade that crossed -4% went on to hit the -8% stop, so the student moved to a 4% stop plus a time stop.
Slice the data for small edges: his own data showed a 45% win rate on trades taken before 10am against 20% between 12pm and 2pm.
Study the losers, not only the winners: check whether most failed to move in your favour within T+3 days; if so, that is a reason to exit such trades earlier.

AI method (2025): gather at least 1 year (preferably 3) of trades, mark the 5%+ moves you captured on an index chart such as NIFTY or NIFTYMIDSML400 with the 10 and 20 MA, upload it to ChatGPT and ask when the market offers easy money.
AI then showed all his large winners had at least 1.5x average volume by the close of the trade day; AARTIPHARM broke out on only 1.1x and cracked, which saved him money.
Knowing how your winners behave lets you cut early: on NETWEB he closed half and lost 0.4% instead of the planned 1%, because his winners do not take long to work.
In 2026 he built a performance dashboard with Claude (avg winner 6.12R, avg loser 0.79R across 20 trade ideas) and says his average loser is under 1R.

lessons.when: An ongoing habit: log each trade as it happens and review the record periodically.

mistakes.text: Not keeping a journal, so you never find out what is working for you.
Studying only winners and ignoring losers.
Spending energy on finding new trades instead of fixing your trading problems.

lessons.evolution: The habit is constant; the tools changed. 2021: manual review of trade data (2021: 1443519340117053446, 1440950564553068548). 2025: uploads marked charts to ChatGPT to find patterns (2025: 1901532635228455182, 1902018549327044838). 2026: performance dashboard built with Claude (2026: 2045025591796404568).

examples.caption: A phone note titled 'Study of first 50 Trades in WTS': of 16 1R trades 8 came in week one and 7 in week two; 25 losing/breakeven trades averaged 9 days; trades past -4% all hit -8%. Conclusions written as a time stop (7 > 9 > 14 days) and a new initial stop of -4%.
Nifty 50 daily (Jul-Aug) with 10 and 20 MAs, annotated with captured moves (e.g. ELGIEQUIP 40.40%, ASAHIINDIA 20.66%, PAYTM 13.42%) - the sample chart for his AI journal exercise.
AARTI PHARMALABS daily: breakout candle on 17 Mar 2025 with volume annotated 'Barely above the average', the trade he flagged after AI showed his big winners needed 1.5x volume.
'Trading Performance Highlights' dashboard: avg winner 6.12R, avg loser 0.79R, win/loss ratio 7.8x, with best setups listed (e.g. 'Hold 4-7 days' profit factor 12.49x).

lessons.title: Study Past Winners to Train the Eye
lessons.rule: His scan is his trained eye, and the eye is trained by studying history: look at a lot of charts, save textbook breakouts in a file, and build a database of past great winners. There are no shortcuts.

how.text: Study history: look at 500+ charts a week to train your eyes to spot good setups in real time.
Save textbook breakouts into a file and memorise them.
Build a playbook or database of great winners of the past; he says all your answers are in it.

For each past winner note: prior uptrend %, consolidation length and depth, consolidation quality, % rise when the trend resumed with its angle and length, volume before and after, and RS against the index.
The payoff: he looks at his 300-400 most liquid stocks daily in under 30 minutes because his eyes are trained, and says he does not depend on a scanner.

lessons.when: Outside market hours; he suggests using the time saved by not scanning daily for studying past winning setups.

mistakes.text: Looking for shortcuts instead of putting in the chart study.
Paying to learn and still skipping the grind of building a database of past winners.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets. The 2021 'save it to your file' habit (2021: 1457951512009723906) became an explicit 2025 checklist for deep dives on past winners (2025: 1960615536317923439).

examples.caption: VIP INDUSTRIES daily, 16 Sep 2021: a tight range near the highs with a dashed 'Buy line' at 487.50, a rising MA beneath, and the breakout bar marked with a green arrow - the 'textbook clean set-up' he saved.
MINDTREE daily, Nov 2021: steep Aug-Sep advance, a sideways base riding the rising MA, and a breakout over a drawn line marked with a green arrow.

lessons.title: Chart and Screen Set-Up: Compressed Bars, Matching MA Periods, No Index on Screen, Inverted Charts
lessons.rule: A few practical habits for reading charts: compress the bars so the pivot is easier to see, convert moving-average periods when changing timeframe, keep indices off your screen if you do not trade them, and invert a chart to read a downtrend with fresh eyes. He also says the small choices people obsess over matter far less than discipline.

how.text: Compress the bars on TradingView by adjusting the price scale; in some cases the entry point becomes much easier to spot. He calls it a superficial hack that works for him: try it or dump it.
Convert the MA period when you change timeframe: 200 MA on the daily is roughly the 40 MA on the weekly.
To improve trade management, remove every index from your screen for two weeks; you do not need indices on screen if you are not trading them.
Invert the chart (Alt+I) when it helps: he inverted an index chart because most people read uptrends well, and took a MARUTI trade from an inverted chart with no indicator.
He uses paint bars on price and volume and says he cannot go back to normal bars.

Equipment: invest in charting software so you can flip through hundreds of stocks quickly; he uses one Dell ultrawide screen, not a multi-monitor setup, and says big screens are not a necessity at the start.

lessons.when: Standard set-up for daily chart review and live trading.

mistakes.text: Forgetting to change the MA period when moving from daily to weekly.
Obsessing over simple vs exponential or 20 vs 21 MA; what matters is discipline, buying more of what works and cutting what does not.

lessons.evolution: No clear change in the tweets. The inverted-chart idea appears in 2022 and again in 2026 (2022: 1501118093086855169, 2026: 2042531295482515487); paint bars are mentioned from 2025 (2025: 1891029986280198549).

examples.caption: JAMNAAUTO daily OHLC bars (May-Jul 2021) at a normal price scale: the base looks like wide swings.
The same JAMNAAUTO chart with the price scale stretched so the bars are compressed: the flat base and the pivot near 86.45 (dashed line) stand out.
His 24 Mar 2026 club update: he inverted the index chart (Alt+I), noting the largest bar and a rally 4 bases old, kept the environment YELLOW and exposure at 20-40%.

lessons.title: The Purple Dot (Combined Up Down with Volume Indicator)
lessons.rule: The Purple Dot marks a day when a stock moves 5% up or down with 500,000+ volume (both customisable). He released it free on TradingView in March 2025 as the 'Combined Up Down with Volume Indicator'. More dots mean a liquid, fast-moving stock; fewer dots mean a slower one.

how.text: What it marks: a purple dot when the stock moves 5% up or down on 500,000+ volume, with an option to customise the thresholds.
How to read it: more dots = high liquidity and fast movement; fewer dots = a slower-moving stock.
Adding it: he shared videos in Aug and Oct 2022 on how to add it; since Mar 2025 it is free on TradingView.
He points to the dots as part of his trade reasoning ('Hint: Purple dots' on the EASEMYTRIP trade) and noted when a dot printed on a new high.
The dots appear on his shared charts from 2021 onward, e.g. under big up days in VIP, Mindtree and Titagarh Wagons.

lessons.when: On his daily charts, as a quick read of how often and how hard a stock moves.
lessons.evolution: Dots already appear on his charts in 2021 (2021: 1438362741475930117); he shared how to add it in 2022 videos (2022: 1560644935598370822, 1581551105896747009) and released it free on TradingView in March 2025 (2025: 1903689654307598536).

examples.caption: GABRIEL INDIA daily (Oct 2024-Mar 2025) from the release tweet: purple dots sit under the few large up candles (Dec, late Jan, early Feb, March), showing where the stock made its big moves.
EASY TRIP PLANNERS daily, 21 Sep 2022: purple dots under the wide-range days in Aug and Sep and under the day pushing to a new high at 432.90, marked with a green arrow.
TITAGARH WAGONS daily, Aug 2022 entry chart: two purple dots under the big early-July and 20-July up days; entry arrow on 19 Aug.
Title card for his Aug 2022 video: 'How to add the now famous Purple Dot marker'.

lessons.title: Prepare Watchlists Out of Hours, Grouped by Setup
lessons.rule: Make the list outside market hours and trade from it, rather than hunting for names live. He keeps separate lists by setup type, such as reversal versus continuation, and uses tools like the Strong Start dashboard only on a short list of names already studied.

how.text: Make the list in the evening for the next day; his trades come from that list.

Keep lists by setup: he compared his reversal watchlist with his continuation watchlist on the same day to see where the money flowed, and leaned on the reversal list when breadth favoured a reversal day.
Easy scan for the reversal list: stocks down the most in a week or a month.
Do not rebuild the watchlist every day; the same names keep repeating, so pick 10-15 good names over the weekend and use that list all week.
Use the Strong Start RVOL dashboard on a focus list of 7-10 names you have already studied, not on the whole market.

lessons.when: Evenings and weekends; the list is used during the week.

mistakes.text: Pointing a live strength scanner at the whole market: it creates FOMO and entries with no prior study or conviction; he says buying what Spider showed as big buying did not make him money.
Running scans every day.

lessons.evolution: 2021: list made each evening for the next day (2021: 1386965683464900610). 2023: keeps a list and updates it periodically instead of scanning daily (2023: 1693837790859985200). 2025: one list of 10-15 names picked at the weekend for the whole week (2025: 1947553747002929285).

lessons.title: Order Types, Broker Rules and Data Quality
lessons.rule: Know how your orders and your broker's rules behave, and do not trust free data blindly. He has given specific fixes for stop orders that fail to fill, explained margin rules, and warned that free charting data and TradingView's earnings calendar are often wrong.

how.text: If a stop order does not execute in a fast fall, keep a wider gap between trigger and limit price, or use an SL-M order, which exits at the next best price - a boon or a bane depending on the situation.
Free charting platforms do not carry accurate tick-by-tick data; he posted his own exchange fill records for a MIRZAINT trade to show this.
Do not rely on TradingView's earnings calendar; he says it has been mostly wrong for years.
Know the margin rules: VAR margin differs by stock (20-100%), and under the 2021 rule BTST needs spare funds or waiting until T+2/T+3 for limits to free up.
He prefers swing cash trades partly because of events like exchange halts, and welcomed the move to T+1 settlement.

lessons.when: Whenever placing orders or checking data.

mistakes.text: Casual risk management: NDTV fell around 10% in a minute and a GTT stop failed to execute.
Judging trade volume from free chart data.

lessons.title: Scans He Uses: 52-Week Highs, Reversal Lists, RS Lists and Ratio Charts
lessons.rule: Scans feed his list; they are not his edge. The one scan he says every big winner gets caught in is the 52-week-high scan, and names that appear on it often are a plus. He also keeps relative-strength lists and has a video on finding leaders with ratio charts.

how.text: Run the 52-week-high scan and keep collecting the names making new 52-week highs; a name appearing often is a big plus.
His TradingView screener settings for it: NSE common stock, 60-day average volume from 100K, price above 30, new 52-week high, current trading day. He runs his scans after the close.
A strong name will show up across many scans at once (high volume, 1-month high, 5%+); he tries to spot it before it gets crowded.
A stock making a new 52-week high while the market is at a 52-week low 'can't be a fluke'.
He shares lists of stocks showing relative strength and a video on finding leading sectors and stocks with ratio charts; the tweets do not spell out the ratio-chart method.
Scans are not his edge: he has made money from 52-week highs, 52-week lows, 1-month highs and names in no scan.

lessons.when: After the close; the output goes into his focus list.

mistakes.text: Getting lost in scans or chasing the perfect scan.
Expecting your scan to produce the same names he buys.

lessons.title: ChartGym: Weekly Annotation of a Past Chart
lessons.rule: ChartGym, started in September 2025, is a weekly workout: he posts a past stock chart and asks you to annotate it as if you were there - where you would enter, exit, put your stop and what you would be thinking - then shares how he would have traded it. The aim is stronger chart reading, sharper trade management and practice with the surprises live markets throw at you.

how.text: Take a past chart over a set window (e.g. MANINDS Feb'23-Feb'24) and mark entry, exit, stop and your thinking at each point.
Then compare with his own walkthrough of how he would have traded it.
A related exercise: run action replay on the last 5-7 days of a chart to see how many attempts a stock made.

He uses what ChartGym shows in live decisions: every ChartGym showed a correction after a 4-bases-old rally, and a ChartGym exercise told him ATHERENERG had high odds of reaching 50%, so he kept trailing it.

lessons.when: Weekly, at weekends.

modules.title: Case studies
modules.intro: Real trades from his logs, entry to exit, tied to the lessons they show.

cases.setup: Weekly Inside Bar (WIB); the same-day second buy was described as a base-on-base breakout with a 4-to-8-week horizon
cases.context: Jan 2021: he was posting that young, low-float companies plus pyramiding and concentration were driving his account.
cases.story: He bought SEQUENT at 173 on 4 Jan 2021, tagging it a weekly inside bar, and added a second equal lot at 179 the same day, calling it a base-on-base breakout he expected to take 4 to 8 weeks. On 7 Jan it made a 52-week high at 192 and that afternoon he closed half at 187, citing a sharp rejection on heavy volume. He held the rest as the stock printed 219 (15 Jan) and 235 (3 Feb, results day), then closed everything at 230 on 5 Feb, reporting the trade as 5.25% on the portfolio.
cases.takeaway: A weekly inside bar gave a defined entry; he banked half on a high-volume rejection and let the other half run for a month.
cases.result_note: Blended: half at 187 and half at 230 against an average cost of 176 (two lots at 173 and 179, which he describes as one each).

timeline.text: New long at 173, labelled weekly inside bar.
Second long at 179; base-on-base breakout, 4-8 week view.
Closed half after a big rejection on a high-volume day.
New 52-week high, up 25%+ from first buy.
Moving again, new high; results due that day.

cases.setup: Three Weeks Tight Closes (3WTC) on the weekly chart
cases.context: Jan 2021: he was concentrating in young low-float names and pyramiding (his own posts that month).
cases.story: He bought IIFL at 116 on 22 Jan 2021, citing three weeks of tight weekly closes; the entry chart shows the boxed tight closes near 115.50. On 29 Jan, results day, it was up 8% and he said he was keeping a strict stop because of the announcement. After results it jumped, he sold 50% at 142.9 and the stock locked a 20% upper circuit. On 1 Feb he sold the rest at 164.5, reporting 4.64% on the portfolio.
cases.takeaway: A tight weekly base gave the entry; through a results day he kept a strict stop, then sold half into the results gap and the rest a session later.
cases.result_note: Half at 142.9 and half at 164.5 against 116.

timeline.text: New long at 116 on weekly tight closes.
Up 8%; strict stop kept as results due today.

cases.setup: Long on a weekly chart holding above its rising average (entry chart, no setup label in the tweet)
cases.context: Mid-March 2021: he said breakouts were not sticking; on 18 Mar three positions closed the same day and he cut risk and benched himself for at least a week.
cases.story: He bought BANCOINDIA at 153 on 15 Mar 2021. It popped 5%+ the same day to 160.5 but did not follow through. On 18 Mar he closed it at 150 for a 0.24% portfolio loss. That same day he posted that breakouts were not sticking, that three positions had closed in one day, and that he was reducing risk and staying out for at least a week.
cases.takeaway: A small loss became a market signal: when several positions close on the same day, he cuts risk and steps aside.

timeline.text: Breakouts not sticking; 3 positions closed same day; reduced risk, benched for a week.

cases.setup: Small base-on-base plus a strong start on the entry day
cases.context: Late March 2022 was choppy for him: two earlier NTPC attempts (23 and 24 Mar) were closed within a day for no momentum, and on 29 Mar he said nothing was working and he was reducing size.
cases.story: After two failed NTPC attempts on 23 and 24 Mar, he bought again on 31 Mar 2022 at 135; a broker screenshot shows 55,000 shares at about 135.10. He said it was a small base-on-base with a strong start, and it gapped up the next day. On 4 Apr he sold some at 144.70 (7R), on 5 Apr sold more as it hit 150, and on 7 Apr sold a large part at 157 (a screenshot shows 30,000 shares at 157.05), calling it 22R and keeping a small part. He later linked that exit to knowing what an abnormal move looks like and to his breadth sheet. On 18 Apr it made a new high at 160 with the rest under a 1% stop, on 19 Apr he sold more at 165.50 (22.5R), and on 10 May he added again with a 2-point stop as it broke out in a weak market.
cases.takeaway: Big size on a tight stop turned a 16% move into 22R; he sold most into an abnormal move and kept a small piece.
cases.result_note: Not computable: several partial sizes are unstated and the final exit is not in the archive. Individual exits ranged from +7% (144.70) to +22.6% (165.50) on the 135 entry.

timeline.text: Bought day before on base-on-base + strong start; gap up today.
Sold more into strength as it reached 150.
22R; sold a large part, kept a small part.
New high; rest held with 1% stop; 18R.
Added with a 2-point stop on a breakout in a weak market.

cases.setup: Short in a slow stage 3 with repeated false breakouts after a strong stage 2 (his words)
cases.context: July 2022: he described breakouts repeatedly failing to follow through and traded very small.
cases.story: On 6 Jul 2022 he posted the reason for a TVS Motor futures short: a slow stage 3 full of false breakouts after a strong stage 2 rally, which he hoped would turn into a stage 4 fall. The opening tweet with the short price is not in the archive. On 7 Jul he said he was out for now (screenshot: bought back at 833.00), and later that day re-shorted (screenshots show sells at 829.20 and 832.15). No later update or exit for the re-entered short appears in the archive.
cases.takeaway: He shorts a topping stage 3 only on his own structure read, and re-enters the same idea immediately after a scratch.
cases.result_note: First short's entry price and the re-entry's exit are not in the archive.

timeline.text: Stage 3 with false breakouts after stage 2; hoping for stage 4.

cases.setup: Reversal Play: anticipation buy after an extended fall on the daily and 30-minute charts
cases.context: Mid-Feb 2022: after many stops hit on 18 Jan he called a change in character; he was playing smaller and shifting to reversal trades.
cases.story: On 15 Feb 2022 he bought JSL at 187.5 with a 2% stop, explaining that the stock had an extended fall on both the daily and 30-minute charts, so he bought in anticipation of a reversal without waiting for a trigger level. It reached 193.50 and then 198 the same day and he took the full position home. Next morning he sold a third at 201.50 and then closed the remaining two-thirds at 205.50, calling it a 4R trade.
cases.takeaway: A reversal play off an extended fall paid about 4R within one session; he sold into the second day's strength.
cases.result_note: One-third at 201.50 and two-thirds at 205.50 against 187.5 (blended 204.17).

timeline.text: Extended fall on daily and 30-min; bought in anticipation.
Beautiful reversal; taking full position home.

cases.setup: Long on a turn up inside a months-long range (entry chart); no setup label in the tweets
cases.context: Jan 2023: he said most breakouts were fading and he was keeping losses small.
cases.story: He bought KPITTECH at 696 on 6 Jan 2023 with a 1% stop. Within half an hour it was 714 on a day Nifty fell 1%, and he added at 716. On 9 Jan he sold 20% at 752, which he called 8 times risk, and later that day closed 50% of the position at an average of 729.8. No exit for the remaining part appears in the thread.

cases.setup: Long with a low-of-day stop (72.30) above a late-December swing low (entry chart); no pattern named

cases.story: He bought RVNL at 73.10 on 12 Jan 2023 with a low-of-day stop at 72.30. It was 75.40 (about 3R) within minutes and hit a 5% upper circuit at 75.80 later that day. On 13 Jan he sold half at 78.20, which he called 6.4 times risk, and the stock hit a second 5% upper circuit at 79.55. On 16 Jan he sold the rest at 79.

cases.result_note: Half at 78.20 and half at 79 against 73.10.

cases.context: Jan 2023: choppy, most breakouts fading by his account.
cases.story: He bought 1,200 BAJFINANCE at 5879.5 on 12 Jan 2023 with a 0.5% stop as a reversal play. Eight minutes later he sold a third at 5954, calling it 3 times risk, and moved the stop on the rest to cost. Three hours later he closed fully, saying it reversed but failed to stay up. The broker screenshot shows all 1,200 sold at an average of 5921.60.
cases.takeaway: Take a quick partial, move the stop to cost, and close the same day if the reversal cannot hold.

Closed fully; reversed but failed to stay up.

cases.setup: Starter position inside a sideways range that had held since mid-December (entry chart); he later called it a seed-stage type buy
cases.context: Early-to-mid Jan 2024: he called the market overheated and warned against big size; on 19 Jan he called MIRZAINT his cash cow in a volatile market.
cases.story: He bought MIRZAINT at 48 on 5 Jan 2024 with a 47 stop as a starter; the screenshot shows 74,000 shares at 48.03. It hit 53.4 within an hour and closed at a 20% upper circuit of 56.6 on day one; he held all. He held all 74,000 through 60 (8 Jan), a new high at 61.25 (16 Jan) and 63+ (19 Jan). On 2 Feb he said the stock had been moved to the trade-for-trade segment, which drains liquidity, so he sold some the previous day and the rest that day; his 70,000 shares were about a third of the 2 lakh traded.
cases.takeaway: A starter in a quiet range turned into a multi-week hold; he left because a regulatory segment change cut liquidity, not because of price.

Cash cow in a volatile market; new highs.
Moved to T2T; sold some on 1 Feb and the balance on 2 Feb.
70,000 of 2 lakh shares traded were his.

Holding all; real-time seed-stage buy example.

cases.setup: Weekly Inside Bars (WIB), a style he said he traded a lot in 2016-2018
cases.context: Jan 2025: weak, choppy market; on 6 Jan he wrote about resisting the urge to book profits while everything else was falling.
cases.story: He bought 4,500 AEGISLOG at 831 on 6 Jan 2025 with a 2% stop. Within 90 minutes it ran through 862, 884 and 902 to 922+, and he called it a risk-free trade while holding all 4,500. On 7 Jan it made a new high, then traded 955 and 1005+, and he posted the WIB weekly chart as his reason. On 10 Jan he wrote that the ride had gone from 831 to 924 to 845 to 1000 and back to 831, and he was out. In a reply he said open gains had exceeded 9 lakh at one point.
cases.takeaway: Making the trade risk-free early meant a full round trip from +20% cost nothing.

831 to 924 to 845 to 1000 and back to 831; out.

cases.setup: 1-hour range break after the largest hourly bar (selling climax)
cases.context: Feb 2026: after a bullish breadth divergence around Budget day he resumed long setups with tight stops, including stock futures.
cases.story: He bought 3,500 IRCTC February futures at 617.05 on 17 Feb 2026 with a 1% stop. In a member post that evening he explained that the ideal entry was the 1-hour range break with a stop below the box, but he spotted it after the close, so he bought in the morning with a stop below the first bar of the day; the largest hourly bar was key. On 19 Feb he sold into strength because expiry was near and no March contract was available; screenshots show two lots of 875 sold at 630.85 and 627.30. On 20 Feb the price was 648 and he posted the reason charts; no exit for the remaining 1,750 is shown.
cases.takeaway: He executed an hourly-chart idea a session late with a tighter first-bar stop, and sold into strength ahead of contract expiry.
cases.result_note: Half (1,750) sold at an average 629.08 = +1.9%; exit of the other half not shown. The 648 was a price update.

timeline.text: 1-hour range break; picked up next morning, stop below first bar; largest hourly bar key.
Selling into strength: expiry near, no March contract (875 at 630.85, 875 at 627.30).

cases.setup: Daily long bias executed on the 1-hour chart: largest red bar (selling climax) followed by a 4-hour range, bought on the range break
cases.context: Feb 2026: index made fresh lows around Budget day while breadth doubled; he read it as bullish divergence. He also cited capital-market stocks ignoring STT news as a reason to size up.
cases.story: He bought 37,500 GROWW at 165.90 on 10 Feb 2026 with a low-of-day stop. His reason: the long bias came from the daily chart and the 1-hour chart was only for execution, where the largest red bar was followed by four hours of range before a break. He added 10,000 at 168.37. On 11 Feb it was 177.5 and he held all 47,500, calling it risk-free; he said capital-market stocks ignoring the STT news increased his conviction. On 12 Feb it hit 181 after squatting hard to a new swing high. A 13 Feb screenshot shows 8,000 sold at 183.01. No further exit appears.
cases.takeaway: Bias from the daily, trigger from the hourly; a selling-climax bar followed by a tight range gave a precise entry.
cases.result_note: Only 8,000 of 47,500 shown sold (183.01, about +10% on the first buy).

timeline.text: Daily bias, 1-hour execution: selling climax then 4-hour range.
Sized up partly because capital-market stocks ignored STT noise.
Squatted hard, back to a new swing high.

cases.setup: Re-entry ('back in this one again') on a pullback to a rising moving average (entry chart)
cases.context: Early Jan 2026: he called it one of the best swing-trading conditions (every index above its 10/20 MA, 1000+ stocks above the 20 MA). The market rolled over from about 9 Jan.

On 8 Jan it was 140.5 and he held all, then posted 'Out' later that day; the screenshot shows 32,000 sold at 132.06.
